detailed_summary: The paper analyzes a quadratic optomechanical system with two spinning resonators near-field coupled to a nanomechanical oscillator. Opposite pump directions acquire different detunings through the Sagnac-Fizeau effect, causing asymmetric intracavity intensities and direction-dependent mechanical frequency shifts via the optical spring effect. With suitable parameters, one direction supports conventional single-phonon blockade while the other supports two-phonon-induced tunneling, with a reported second-order-correlation contrast above 55 dB.
main_result: The scheme predicts strongly nonreciprocal phonon blockade with direction-selective antibunching and bunching behavior.
application_angle: Directional control of phonon statistics is useful for phononic information routing, switches, and hybrid quantum hardware interfaces.

title: Propagation dynamics of high-gain vortex beams in symmetry-broken media via forward and backward three-wave mixing
abstract: In recent years, vortex light, a distinctive form of structured light, has attracted considerable attention owing to its unique properties and the rich physical phenomena arising from its interaction with matter. In this paper, we investigate the propagation dynamics of vortex beams in a symmetry-broken three-level system based on forward and backward three-wave mixing (TWM) processes. We find that both processes enable the transfer of high-gain vortex light, with the associated topological charges obeying identical algebraic relations. The forward process exhibits periodic oscillatory transmission and modulates the transverse spatial profile of the generated signal vortex field, whereas the backward process features stable transmission and produces a signal field with higher gain and improved fidelity. Under the Autler-Townes splitting (ATS) regime, the probe field detuning in both schemes has a negligible influence on the gain. Optical depth influences only the rate at which the gain approaches its maximum, while the peak value remains unchanged. These results constitute a meaningful extension of the work reported in reference [40] and may provide a feasible approach for quantum communication, quantum computation, and the generation of high-gain, high-fidelity vortex light.
one_liner: Studies high-gain vortex-beam transfer in symmetry-broken three-level media via forward and backward three-wave mixing.
why_it_matters: High-fidelity transfer of orbital-angular-momentum light is relevant for structured-light quantum communication channels.
detailed_summary: The authors model vortex-beam propagation in a symmetry-broken three-level system using forward and backward three-wave mixing. Both processes transfer high-gain vortex light with matching algebraic relations for topological charge, but their propagation behavior differs. The backward process is predicted to provide more stable transmission, higher gain, and better fidelity, while detuning has little effect under the Autler-Townes splitting regime.
main_result: Backward three-wave mixing is predicted to generate higher-gain, higher-fidelity vortex signal fields than the forward process.
application_angle: Robust generation and transfer of vortex light can support OAM-based quantum communication and structured-light processing.

title: Construction of a Class of Communication-Efficient Quantum Secret Sharing Schemes
abstract: Quantum secret sharing is a fundamental technique in quantum cryptography. However, in practical quantum networks, it still faces several bottlenecks, such as high quantum communication cost and low transmission efficiency. To reduce the communication cost, ramp quantum secret sharing schemes have been proposed in existing studies. Nevertheless, intermediate sets in such schemes may leak partial information about the secret. To address this problem, this paper presents a method for detecting intermediate sets. Based on this method, we further propose a communication-efficient perfect quantum secret sharing scheme with eavesdropping detection capability.We analyze the communication cost under different numbers of participating parties and determine the range of participants that minimizes the reconstruction communication cost. The results verify the communication efficiency and security of the proposed scheme.
one_liner: Constructs communication-efficient perfect quantum secret-sharing schemes with intermediate-set detection and eavesdropping checks.
why_it_matters: Reducing reconstruction communication cost while avoiding partial leakage addresses a practical bottleneck for quantum network cryptography.
detailed_summary: The paper targets the communication overhead and leakage risks in practical quantum secret-sharing networks. It introduces a method for detecting intermediate sets that could otherwise learn partial information in ramp schemes. Building on that method, it proposes a perfect quantum secret-sharing construction with eavesdropping detection and analyzes participant regimes that minimize reconstruction communication cost.
main_result: The authors present a perfect quantum secret-sharing scheme designed to reduce communication cost while detecting eavesdropping and intermediate-set leakage.
application_angle: The construction is aimed at more efficient and secure multiparty secret reconstruction in quantum communication networks.

title: Physics-Informed Graph Neural Networks for Surface Code Decoding via Discrete Exterior Calculus
abstract: We introduce a physics-informed graph neural network decoder for the surface code. A discrete Poisson equation on the syndrome graph acts as a hard inductive bias on which a graph encoder learns syndrome-adaptive edge weights. A differentiable solver returns the node potentials and the associated edge current. Our central observation is that the logical-error signal is not carried by any part of that current, but by how the syndrome sits relative to the two code boundaries. We place a sink on each of the two boundaries linked by the logical operator and read the difference of the currents they drain. We prove that this single number is a topological pairing: it weighs each excited detector by a smooth coordinate that runs from +1 on one boundary to -1 on the other, and sums the votes. The coordinate is fixed by both the code topology and the learned metric, generating an exact and free-parameter readout. On the rotated surface code under circuit-level depolarising noise, this one topological scalar matches the best full-field readout. That parity is itself the result: for one logical qubit the logical signal is one-dimensional, so projecting onto it discards nothing. At larger code distance the picture strengthens indicating that isolating the pairing helps more as the field grows larger and sparser.
one_liner: Introduces a physics-informed GNN surface-code decoder using discrete exterior calculus and a topological boundary-current readout.
why_it_matters: Improved, structured decoding methods are central to scalable fault-tolerant quantum hardware with surface codes.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a graph neural network decoder for surface codes with a hard inductive bias from a discrete Poisson equation on the syndrome graph. A learned metric produces node potentials and edge currents, but the logical signal is read from a single topological scalar: the difference between currents drained at the two logical boundaries. For rotated surface codes under circuit-level depolarizing noise, this readout matches the best full-field readout and appears to improve with larger, sparser code distances.
main_result: A single learned topological boundary-current scalar is shown to match full-field readout performance for one logical qubit decoding.
application_angle: The approach could make neural decoders more interpretable and efficient for fault-tolerant quantum computing hardware.

title: Intermittency in Quantum Graviton-Phonon Conversion
abstract: A graviton can be converted into a phonon in a resonant bar detector. First-order perturbation theory predicts a strong enhancement of this conversion for coherent and squeezed graviton states, but the probability can exceed unity when the coherent or squeezing parameter is large. Since a conversion probability must satisfy the unitarity bound, we solve the graviton-phonon quantum dynamics exactly within the rotating-wave approximation. For an initial coherent state, we find that the conversion occurs intermittently through narrow bursts separated by intervals of strong suppression. For an initial squeezed state, the departure from perturbative behavior occurs earlier, and the conversion is strongly suppressed after its initial growth. These effects may provide signatures of quantum graviton-phonon dynamics relevant to single-graviton detection.
one_liner: Exact graviton-phonon dynamics predict bursty, unitary conversion beyond perturbation theory in resonant bar detectors.
why_it_matters: It reframes proposed single-graviton detection signatures by showing coherent or squeezed inputs can produce intermittent or suppressed conversion, not simple enhancement.
detailed_summary: The paper solves resonant graviton-to-phonon conversion exactly within the rotating-wave approximation to restore unitary behavior where first-order perturbation theory can exceed probability one. Coherent graviton inputs yield narrow conversion bursts separated by suppressed intervals, while squeezed inputs leave the perturbative regime earlier and become strongly suppressed after initial growth. These predicted temporal signatures could inform how macroscopic mechanical detectors search for quantum gravitational excitations.
main_result: Exact quantum dynamics show graviton-phonon conversion becomes intermittent or suppressed at large coherent or squeezing parameters.
application_angle: The work identifies nonperturbative timing signatures that could guide single-graviton sensing protocols in mechanical resonant detectors.

title: Biased-noise qubits: a guide to efficient fault-tolerance using the hierarchy of errors
abstract: Qubits with strongly biased noise, in which phase-flip errors are orders of magnitude more frequent than bit-flips, arise both naturally, as in electron and nuclear spins, and by engineering, as in stabilized cat qubits. This noise structure holds the promise of reducing the daunting hardware overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computing, but exploiting it requires physical operations that do not convert frequent phase-flips into rare bit-flips. In this review, we analyze the most prominent fault-tolerant protocols for biased-noise qubits, organized according to the available set of such bias-preserving operations. When this set is restricted to the CZ gate together with preparation and measurement in the X basis, we show that the complexity of the required syndrome extraction gadgets essentially cancels the benefit of the noise bias: at experimentally relevant error rates, one may as well ignore the bias and rely on standard error correction designed for depolarizing noise. The situation changes drastically when a bias-preserving CX gate is available: the hierarchy of errors can then be reflected in the structure of the code, with frequent phase-flips corrected by a dedicated high-threshold code and rare bit-flips by concatenation with a high-rate code. The same hierarchy also enables hardware-efficient preparation of magic states. Finally, as a bias-preserving CX is forbidden in naturally biased platforms and challenging in engineered ones, we present a measurement-based architecture in which a high-fidelity quantum non-demolition readout of multi-qubit Pauli Z operators takes its place, extending these overhead reductions to a much broader range of physical platforms.
one_liner: A fault-tolerance roadmap shows biased-noise qubits need bias-preserving CX or QND Pauli-Z readout to cut overhead.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when noise bias actually reduces hardware cost and when syndrome gadgets erase the advantage at realistic error rates.
detailed_summary: This review organizes biased-noise fault-tolerant protocols by the available bias-preserving operation set. It argues that CZ plus X-basis preparation and measurement often fails to exploit bias because syndrome-extraction complexity cancels the gain. With bias-preserving CX, or measurement-based replacement via high-fidelity QND multi-qubit Pauli-Z readout, codes can separately handle frequent phase flips and rare bit flips, reducing overhead and enabling efficient magic-state preparation.
main_result: The main result is a hierarchy-based fault-tolerance guide showing overhead reductions require bias-preserving CX or equivalent QND Pauli-Z measurements.
application_angle: It provides architecture-level guidance for cat, spin, and other biased-noise hardware seeking practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Two Complementary Approaches to Determine the Effective Index of Dielectric Ring Resonators
abstract: Open-source finite-element frameworks for modal analysis of dielectric ring resonators are presented based on two complementary approaches. The first computes resonant wavelengths for discrete azimuthal mode numbers and obtains the effective index at a target wavelength by interpolation; the second solves directly for the azimuthal mode number at a prescribed wavelength via a quadratic eigenvalue formulation. Both approaches are validated against a commercial electromagnetic mode solver and yield nearly identical effective indices and dispersion curves. The fixed-mode-number approach requires slightly longer computation time but uses half as much memory, making it the preferred choice for memory-limited computers.
one_liner: Open-source FEM methods extract effective index and dispersion of dielectric ring resonators with commercial-solver agreement.
why_it_matters: Reliable, accessible modal-analysis tools lower the barrier to designing integrated photonic resonators for sensing and quantum photonics.
detailed_summary: The authors present two finite-element workflows for dielectric ring resonator modal analysis: interpolation from discrete azimuthal mode resonances and direct solution for the mode number at a fixed wavelength. Both approaches reproduce commercial electromagnetic solver results and give nearly identical effective indices and dispersion curves. The fixed-mode-number method is somewhat slower but uses roughly half the memory, making it useful on constrained machines.
main_result: Two open-source FEM formulations accurately determine ring-resonator effective index and dispersion with validated agreement against commercial simulation.
application_angle: The methods support practical photonic component design where resonator dispersion and modal index must be optimized without proprietary tools.

title: Mesoscopic mechanical superpositions by gluing individual quantum systems
abstract: We propose a protocol for preparing mechanical Schrödinger kittens -- mesoscopic quantum superpositions of coherent motional states of an optically levitated nanoparticle -- by adhering single electron time-bin states to its surface. Over short protocol timescales, coherence of the mesoscopic superposition survives the dominant decoherence mechanisms afflicting levitated systems, and can be observed by varying the phase of the time-bin electrons. Interference fringes can be detected with real-time, near-Heisenberg limited interferometry of photons scattered from the particle. This approach eliminates the need for coherent state expansion, dark potentials, and particle release-and-recapture mechanisms, providing a new route to test quantum mechanics in unprecedented scales.
one_liner: A levitated nanoparticle protocol creates mechanical Schrödinger kittens by attaching single-electron time-bin states.
why_it_matters: It offers a route to mesoscopic motional superpositions without release-recapture, dark potentials, or coherent-state expansion.
detailed_summary: The proposal prepares mesoscopic motional superpositions of an optically levitated nanoparticle by adhering single electron time-bin states to its surface. Over short protocol durations, the superposition coherence is predicted to survive dominant levitated-system decoherence channels. The phase-dependent interference can be read out using near-Heisenberg-limited real-time interferometry of photons scattered from the particle.
main_result: The protocol predicts observable mesoscopic mechanical superpositions generated by coupling electron time-bin states to nanoparticle motion.
application_angle: It could enable tabletop tests of quantum mechanics at larger masses and improve quantum sensing protocols based on levitated mechanics.

title: Observable Geometry for Effective Quantum Circuits
abstract: We study redundancy and effectiveness of Variational Quantum Circuits via algebraic and geometric views of Lie groups. Considering unitary transformations acting on Hermitian observables, a stabilizer group decomposition is given. Subsequently, we identify the Hermitian orbit with a quotient space of a symmetric space. Through this connection, we characterize the effective circuit degrees of freedom. Our approach of spectral decompositions and homogeneous spaces yields tractable calculation criteria, which are verified by numerical experiments.
one_liner: Lie-group geometry identifies the effective degrees of freedom in variational quantum circuits acting on observables.
why_it_matters: Reducing redundant circuit parameters can make variational algorithms more trainable and hardware-efficient.
detailed_summary: The paper studies variational quantum circuit redundancy through algebraic and geometric structure of unitary actions on Hermitian observables. It introduces a stabilizer-group decomposition and connects Hermitian orbits to quotient spaces of symmetric spaces. These tools yield calculable criteria for the effective circuit degrees of freedom, supported by numerical experiments.
main_result: The work provides geometric criteria to count and characterize nonredundant degrees of freedom in observable-driven quantum circuits.
application_angle: The framework can guide compact ansatz design for near-term quantum hardware by avoiding parameters that do not change measured observables.

title: Entanglement dynamics through electromagnetic interactions in single-electron traps
abstract: We study the dynamics of quantum entanglement between two harmonically trapped electrons interacting via the electromagnetic force. Starting from two-mode Gaussian states at thermal equilibrium, we make use of the covariance matrix formalism in order to compute the logarithmic negativity of the evolved state as a quantitative measure of entanglement. We analyze two initial configurations: thermal single-mode and two-mode squeezed states, and describe the time evolution of entanglement in the system for different values of squeezing and temperature, while identifying the parameter regimes accessible to current and near-future single-electron trap experiments.
one_liner: Covariance-matrix simulations map entanglement generation between two trapped electrons coupled electromagnetically.
why_it_matters: It identifies experimentally accessible regimes for observing motional entanglement in single-electron trap hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper models two harmonically trapped electrons interacting through the electromagnetic force using Gaussian covariance-matrix dynamics. It computes logarithmic negativity for thermal single-mode and two-mode squeezed initial states across squeezing and temperature parameters. The analysis highlights parameter regimes reachable by current and near-future single-electron trap experiments.
main_result: The study predicts when electromagnetic coupling can dynamically generate or preserve entanglement between trapped-electron motional modes.
application_angle: The results support trapped-electron platforms for quantum hardware experiments and precision tests using controllable mesoscopic entanglement.

title: Microwave-driven same-species sympathetic cooling for trapped ions
abstract: Sympathetic cooling of data qubits by coolant ions is an essential technique for trapped-ion quantum computing. Conventionally a second ion species is used, requiring additional lasers and complicating optical setups. We propose a scheme for sympathetic cooling using the same species and test it for $^{43}$Ca$^+$ ions. Pulsed sideband cooling and ion addressing are implemented via integrated microwave control, further simplifying optical requirements. We cool a two-ion gate mode close to its ground state ($\bar{n}\approx 0.16$) and benchmark an induced error on the data qubit of $1.7(4)\times 10^{-4}$ per cooling cycle.
one_liner: Same-species trapped-ion sympathetic cooling is demonstrated using integrated microwave control in 43Ca+ two-ion chains.
why_it_matters: It reduces laser and species complexity for ion processors while keeping cooling-induced data-qubit error near 1e-4 per cycle.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes and tests same-species sympathetic cooling for trapped-ion quantum computing, avoiding the extra lasers and optical complexity of dual-species coolant schemes. In a two-ion 43Ca+ system, pulsed sideband cooling and ion addressing are implemented with integrated microwave control. A two-ion gate mode is cooled close to the ground state with mean occupation about 0.16, while the induced data-qubit error is benchmarked at 1.7(4)e-4 per cooling cycle.
main_result: The work demonstrates microwave-driven same-species sympathetic cooling of a gate mode to nbar about 0.16 with 1.7(4)e-4 data-qubit error per cycle.
application_angle: The approach could simplify scalable trapped-ion modules by reducing species-dependent laser infrastructure and coolant overhead.

title: Statevector-Referenced Geometry Survival of a Four-Qubit ZZ Quantum Kernel on IBM Quantum Hardware: A Fixed-Subset Diagnostic Across Three Execution Configurations
abstract: Quantum-kernel methods encode a dataset's geometry in a Gram matrix, so learning claims on hardware kernels assume the intended geometry survives execution. We measure that survival for one frozen four-qubit ZZ feature-map kernel on $N=24$ real indoor air-quality windows, reconstructed on ibm_fez (1024 shots per circuit) under baseline, dynamical decoupling alone, and gate twirling alone, each a single non-interleaved job. Every configuration returned a complete, finite, positive-semidefinite Gram matrix and preserved the centered statevector geometry to a substantial but incomplete descriptive degree (full-matrix centered kernel alignment, CKA, 0.933-0.989). Gate twirling was most faithful on every reported geometry axis, with the only jackknife-resolved improvement over baseline (persisted Spearman, mean absolute error, and full-matrix CKA diagnostics); dynamical decoupling alone was not separated from baseline at the frozen-window scale. Residual hardware distortion, not finite sampling, dominates the discrepancy. Yet fidelity and label alignment were reversed: the most faithful configuration had the lowest centered kernel-target alignment, which sits at or below label-permutation references for statevector and hardware alike. We read the small hardware uplift as a normalization property of the non-affine distortion, not captured signal. These are descriptive results for single jobs on one backend, not causal mitigation-efficacy estimates; no quantum-advantage, hardware-classifier-superiority, or forecasting claim is made. Implementation fidelity and task relevance are distinct axes; hardware quantum machine-learning studies should report both.
one_liner: A four-qubit ZZ quantum kernel on IBM hardware is benchmarked against statevector geometry across mitigation settings.
why_it_matters: It separates hardware implementation fidelity from downstream task relevance, a useful diagnostic for near-term quantum ML claims.
detailed_summary: The study reconstructs a frozen four-qubit ZZ feature-map Gram matrix for 24 indoor air-quality windows on ibm_fez using baseline execution, dynamical decoupling, and gate twirling. All runs produce finite positive-semidefinite kernels and preserve centered statevector geometry with full-matrix CKA values from 0.933 to 0.989. Gate twirling is most faithful on the reported geometry metrics, but the most faithful hardware kernel has the lowest centered kernel-target alignment, emphasizing that faithful implementation and label utility are distinct.
main_result: Gate twirling gives the strongest measured geometry preservation, while residual hardware distortion dominates over finite-shot sampling error.
application_angle: The diagnostic framework is relevant for sensor-data quantum ML studies because it checks whether hardware kernels preserve geometry and whether that geometry is task-useful.

title: Qoreo: Choreographic Programming for Quantum Distributed Systems
abstract: Programming distributed quantum systems requires multiple actors to coordinate precise sequences of quantum operations, classical communication, and entanglement generation. Writing such protocols directly as distributed processes is tedious and error-prone, and subtle mismatches can cause deadlock or silently incorrect quantum states. We present Qoreo, a choreographic programming language for quantum distributed systems in which an entire protocol is expressed as single, global program (a choreography) rather than as a collection of independent actor processes. Qoreo includes a local quantum language with linear types that enforce the no-cloning principle; a choreographic language that combines local quantum computation with inter-actor classical and quantum communication; and a process language for individual network nodes. We prove type safety for choreographies, guaranteeing that well-typed programs implement well-defined quantum operations, and we define endpoint projection~(EPP), which automatically derives a network of independent processes from any choreography. We prove EPP sound and complete with respect to the choreographic semantics; as a corollary, every well-typed choreography projects to a deadlock-free process network. The metatheory of Qoreo is fully mechanized in Rocq, and we provide an extraction pipeline to NetQASM for simulation and deployment on quantum network hardware.
one_liner: Qoreo specifies distributed quantum protocols as global choreographies and projects them into deadlock-free node processes.
why_it_matters: It targets a core software reliability gap for quantum networks: coordinating quantum operations, entanglement, and classical messaging safely.
detailed_summary: Qoreo is a choreographic programming language for quantum distributed systems, allowing a whole protocol to be written as one global program rather than separate node scripts. Its local quantum language uses linear types to enforce no-cloning, while the choreographic layer combines local computation with classical and quantum communication. The authors prove type safety plus endpoint-projection soundness and completeness, mechanize the metatheory in Rocq, and provide extraction to NetQASM for simulation and hardware-oriented deployment.
main_result: The paper provides a type-safe choreography language whose well-typed programs project to deadlock-free process networks with NetQASM extraction.
application_angle: This can make quantum network protocol development less error-prone and more portable across simulators and emerging network hardware.

title: Fermionic pairs, from the surface to the bulk
abstract: Fermion pairing underlies collective quantum phenomena across widely different forms of matter. In extended systems such as ultracold Fermi gases, pairing is commonly understood through the BCS--BEC crossover, where the pair size evolves from large, overlapping Cooper pairs to tightly bound dimers. In finite systems such as atomic nuclei, superconducting grains and quantum dots, however, the same pairing tendency competes with confinement, shell filling and spatial inhomogeneity, making the microscopic structure of pairs much harder to access. Here, we image pair correlations in a finite, tunable system of few fermionic atoms with single-particle resolution and full counting statistics. We observe that confinement and shell structure re-organize pairing in real space: In the weakly interacting, confinement-dominated regime, closed-shell configurations suppress correlations in the high-density trap center. Pairing is mainly observed toward the low-density surface. Open-shell systems, however, support substantially stronger central pairing. Already for surprisingly small systems, increasing either interaction strength or particle number restores a locally bulk-like Cooper-pair profile in the trap center, whereas the edge retains dimer-like correlations. By resolving where pairs form and how their character changes from localized dimers to overlapping Cooper pairs, our measurements provide a microscopic view of pairing in finite fermionic matter and connect the physics of mesoscopic cold atoms to pairing phenomena in nuclei and superconducting nanostructures.
one_liner: Few-fermion pair correlations are imaged with single-particle resolution from surface-dominated to bulk-like regimes.
why_it_matters: It gives direct microscopic access to finite-system pairing, linking cold-atom control to nuclei, grains, quantum dots, and nanostructures.
detailed_summary: The work images pair correlations in finite, tunable few-fermion atomic systems using single-particle resolution and full counting statistics. It shows that confinement and shell filling reorganize where pairing appears: closed shells suppress central correlations in weak interactions, while open shells enhance central pairing. Increasing interaction strength or particle number restores a locally bulk-like Cooper-pair profile in the trap center, with more dimer-like correlations persisting near the edge.
main_result: The experiment spatially resolves how fermion pairs move from surface-dominated correlations to bulk-like Cooper-pair profiles as interactions and particle number grow.
application_angle: The measurements provide a controllable quantum simulator for pairing physics relevant to mesoscopic matter, nuclei, and superconducting nanostructures.

title: Enabling Neutral Atom Integration: Redesigning Device Models for Universal Quantum Ecosystems
abstract: Quantum computing is transitioning from an academic idea to a practical technology, driven by recent hardware advancements and clear paths toward real-world applications. Universal quantum ecosystems (e.g., Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane) facilitate this transition by providing a consistent interface to diverse quantum devices, abstracting hardware-specific details through a device model that captures each device's computational capabilities. However, these device models have historically been shaped by superconducting hardware, assuming static qubit positions and fixed coupling maps. This prevents them from representing the unique computational capabilities of emerging technologies such as neutral atoms, which feature dynamic qubit rearrangement and zoned operations. As a result, although numerous specialized compilers for neutral atom devices already exist, they cannot retrieve the hardware information they need through these ecosystems - creating a technology lock that hinders or even prevents the integration of neutral atom devices. In this work, we demonstrate how this limitation leads to suboptimal compilation results and can exclude certain devices entirely. Motivated by this, we propose rethinking current device models to faithfully represent neutral atom devices, enabling their seamless integration into universal quantum ecosystems. Evaluations conducted within the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI) demonstrate that the proposed device model unlocks a routing overhead fidelity improvement by a factor of up to 100,000 on a circuit with 16 qubits and 600 gates.
one_liner: Neutral-atom device models are redesigned so universal quantum SDKs can represent rearrangement and zoned operations.
why_it_matters: Accurate device descriptions can unlock neutral-atom compilation advantages now hidden by superconducting-style static coupling models.
detailed_summary: The paper argues that mainstream quantum ecosystem device models are biased toward superconducting hardware assumptions such as static qubit positions and fixed coupling maps. These abstractions cannot expose neutral-atom capabilities like dynamic rearrangement and zoned operations to compilers. The authors propose richer device models and evaluate them through the Quantum Device Management Interface, showing that better hardware representation can dramatically improve compilation outcomes.
main_result: The proposed device model yields routing-overhead fidelity improvements up to a factor of 100000 on a 16-qubit, 600-gate circuit in QDMI evaluations.
application_angle: It supports practical integration of neutral-atom processors into Qiskit-like universal ecosystems without hiding hardware-native advantages.

title: Finite Key Underwater Quantum Key Distribution: Performance Analysis and Improvements
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) allows for the establishment of a secret key between two parties, secure against computationally unbounded adversaries. Most experimental and theoretical research in this area, investigates the performance of QKD over fiber or free space channels. A growing body of work, however, has begun to investigate its performance in underwater scenarios. Here, we consider the realistic finite key scenario, and evaluate the simulated performance of two different decoy state protocols. We show that there are certain underwater channels where "simpler" QKD protocols outperform more complex ones. Finally, we also investigate methods to improve QKD performance underwater, specifically looking at classical advantage distillation, which we show can greatly improve the maximal distance supported by QKD underwater.
one_liner: Finite-key underwater QKD performance is simulated for decoy protocols and improved using advantage distillation.
why_it_matters: It addresses realistic underwater quantum links where finite data, channel loss, and protocol choice can determine whether secure keys are possible.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes underwater quantum key distribution in the finite-key regime, comparing simulated performance for two decoy-state protocols. It finds that simpler protocols can outperform more complex alternatives for some underwater channel conditions. The study also evaluates classical advantage distillation and shows it can substantially extend the maximum supported underwater QKD distance.
main_result: Finite-key simulations show protocol-dependent underwater QKD performance and demonstrate that advantage distillation can greatly increase achievable range.
application_angle: The results inform secure underwater communications for maritime, sensor-network, and submerged platform links under realistic finite-data constraints.

title: Digitally Programmable Photochromic Hydrogel Contact Lenses as Light-Adaptive Artificial Irises
abstract: Excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation is associated with a range of ocular pathologies, motivating the development of soft optical devices that can dynamically regulate incident light. In the human eye, this adaptive optical functionality is performed by the iris, which modulates pupil size to control retinal irradiance in response to ambient illumination. Here we present a photochromic contact lens based artificial iris that mimics this biological light-adaptation mechanism through reversible, spatially programmable modulation of optical transmission with intrinsic UV blocking. Photochromic dyes are embedded within a biocompatible hydrogel matrix, while the cross-linked network is patterned using a digital micromirror device (DMD)based grayscale UV lithography to encode controlled radial gradients in dye switching. This approach generates iris-like attenuation profiles that emulate pupil-dependent light regulation while enabling customizable iris geometries and transmission patterns. The resulting lenses exhibit rapid and reversible UV-induced darkening with position-dependent kinetics, enabling continuous modulation of transmitted light. The photoresponse remains stable over repeated activation cycles without measurable fatigue. The patterned lenses maintain mechanical stability, controlled swelling, and wettability suitable for contact lens applications. This platform combines programmable photochromism and hydrogel optics to enable light-adaptive lenses that mimic key functions of the human iris.
one_liner: Programmable photochromic hydrogel contact lenses emulate iris-like, UV-triggered adaptive transmission profiles.
why_it_matters: It points toward soft, wearable optical devices that dynamically regulate ocular irradiance while remaining compatible with contact-lens mechanics and wetting.
detailed_summary: The work embeds photochromic dyes in a biocompatible hydrogel and patterns the cross-linked network with DMD grayscale UV lithography. This creates spatially programmable radial gradients in dye switching, producing iris-like attenuation profiles with reversible UV-induced darkening. The lenses retain mechanical stability, controlled swelling, wettability, and stable cycling without measurable fatigue.
main_result: The authors demonstrate digitally patterned hydrogel lenses with rapid, reversible, position-dependent optical transmission modulation and intrinsic UV blocking.
application_angle: The platform could enable wearable light-adaptive contact lenses for retinal irradiance management and ocular UV protection.

title: Component-Level Inverse Design of Transmon Qubits Using Neural Networks
abstract: Designing a superconducting qubit to realize specific Hamiltonian parameters typically requires iterating through a time and compute-intensive forward loop in which the designer chooses a layout geometry, simulates it, extracts circuit parameters such as capacitances, and refines the geometry. We study the inverse version of this task using a neural-network workflow that maps target Hamiltonian parameters directly to component-level layout parameters, which we subsequently demonstrate on a planar transmon layout. During training, we pair the inverse model with a frozen forward surrogate model and evaluate the loss in Hamiltonian space rather than in layout-parameter space. In validation against a conventional EM solver, 97% of generated designs produce usable geometries, and the inverse-plus-surrogate pipeline reaches mean percent errors of 0.73% for qubit frequency and 1.58% for anharmonicity, comparable to or below the fabrication and simulation-to-measurement uncertainty expected for academic-process transmon devices of this type. A single pipeline query takes approximately 56 ms on CPU, versus approximately 2 min for a conventional EM capacitance extraction on the same hardware, a speedup of more than 2,100 times. Batching minimizes the AI model inference overhead, reducing the runtime to 0.24 ms per sample on CPU and 2.5 microseconds per sample on GPU, resulting in speedups of 5.0 x 10^5 and 4.8 x 10^7, respectively, relative to a single conventional CPU EM extraction. Our results indicate that component-level inverse design usefully extends and complements conventional EM simulation, including for small datasets on the order of 1,000 samples.
one_liner: A neural inverse-design workflow maps target transmon Hamiltonian parameters directly to component-level layouts.
why_it_matters: Fast inverse layout generation could compress superconducting-qubit design loops from minutes to milliseconds while staying within practical fabrication uncertainty.
detailed_summary: The paper trains an inverse model paired with a frozen forward surrogate, evaluating loss in Hamiltonian space rather than layout-parameter space. On a planar transmon design task, 97% of generated outputs are usable geometries when checked against a conventional EM solver. The pipeline achieves mean errors of 0.73% in qubit frequency and 1.58% in anharmonicity, with large CPU and GPU speedups over EM capacitance extraction.
main_result: The workflow generates component-level transmon layouts matching target Hamiltonian parameters with sub-2% mean errors and over 2,100x single-query CPU speedup.
application_angle: It can accelerate superconducting processor design, parameter targeting, and layout-space exploration for academic-scale fabrication processes.

title: Absent, Not Faint: Fisher-Information Limits and a Logarithmic Measurement-Design Cure for Passive Characterization of Coherent Qubit Noise
abstract: Calibrating a quantum processor means estimating error parameters, and estimation theory usually assumes a parameter hard to estimate is faint: its signal is weak but present, so more repetitions or a richer model will recover it. This assumption fails for a leading hardware fault. A coherent over-rotation is a small systematic gate miscalibration. Measured through the cheapest data a device returns--one fixed-basis histogram--it is not faint but absent: to first order it leaves the distribution unchanged, indistinguishable from a compensating stochastic error, exactly as two numbers cannot be separated from their sum. For commuting single- and two-qubit transverse over-rotations, with known support on the canonical input, the histogram's Fisher information is singular along the fault's direction at zero angle, its Cramer-Rao bound is infinite, and no finite-variance, locally unbiased estimator recovers it. At a generic nonzero angle the degeneracy partly lifts; beyond four qubits it clears entirely, leaving conditioning, not absence, as the obstruction. The cure is a richer measurement, not a richer model: a fixed, logarithmically small set of extra settings makes every such fault visible. Visibility alone is not enough. The sampling cost is set by conditioning, not coverage, through a floor whose complete-family closed form is exponentially small in the qubit count. We prove the impossibility and cure, confirm both in exact simulation, show conditioning predicts recovery error across hundreds of designs, and observe a 3-5x bias gap on IBM Heron hardware as a consistency check. Non-commuting faults and unknown support remain open.
one_liner: Fixed-basis histograms can make coherent qubit over-rotations statistically absent, not merely weak.
why_it_matters: The result clarifies when cheap characterization data cannot identify coherent hardware faults and gives a compact measurement-design fix.
detailed_summary: The paper shows that for commuting transverse single- and two-qubit over-rotations with known support, a fixed-basis histogram has singular Fisher information at zero angle. In that regime, the coherent fault is indistinguishable to first order from compensating stochastic error, giving an infinite Cramer-Rao bound for locally unbiased estimation. A logarithmically small set of extra measurement settings restores visibility, while conditioning determines the sampling cost; simulations and IBM Heron data support the analysis.
main_result: The authors prove an identifiability failure for passive fixed-basis characterization and show that logarithmically many added settings expose the coherent faults.
application_angle: This informs practical calibration protocols by specifying when extra measurement settings are required to diagnose systematic gate errors.

title: Nonlinear and Quantum Optics with Whispering Gallery Resonators Revisited
abstract: In 2016 we published a review paper "Nonlinear and Quantum Optics with Whispering Gallery Resonators" (1). While writing this review, we found it often necessary to defer addressing many challenges of the field to the future. At the same time, many potential benefits offered by nonlinear optical resonators were also deferred to the future pending the underlying technology development. The past ten years have seen a great deal of such development, including in the field of resonator optics. We feel that an update to our 2016 review is in order. In this new review we focus on the most significant developments in the field that took place in past ten years.
one_liner: A decade-update review surveys major progress in nonlinear and quantum optics using whispering-gallery resonators.
why_it_matters: Whispering-gallery resonators remain central to compact nonlinear optics, precision sensing, frequency conversion, and quantum photonic devices.
detailed_summary: This review revisits the authors' 2016 survey and focuses on significant developments over the following decade. It frames progress in resonator optics around capabilities that were previously deferred pending technology maturation. The scope is especially relevant to nonlinear optical resonators and their quantum-optical applications.
main_result: The paper provides an updated technical review of key advances in nonlinear and quantum optics with whispering-gallery resonators since 2016.
application_angle: It is useful as a roadmap for compact photonic platforms supporting sensing, nonlinear conversion, and quantum-optics applications.

title: Discrete-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution with uncertainty principle
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution is a compelling framework for scalable quantum networks due to its seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. However, a fundamental gap persists between theoretical protocols requiring ideal Gaussian modulation and the constrained, discrete-modulated signals dictated by practical high-speed hardware. Current security proofs for discrete modulation rely on semidefinite programming, which suffers from prohibitive computational overhead for high-order constellations and lacks direct physical insight into non-Gaussian modulation.In this Letter, we overcome this limitation by developing a security framework that obviates semidefinite programming in favor of an approach grounded fundamentally in the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. By introducing a multi-mode entanglement-source model to characterize non-Gaussian state preparation, we establish an explicit mapping between constellation geometry and the secret key rate. This framework effectively quantifies the security implications of hardware-limited, finite state preparation, enabling both numerical and analytical security analysis under high-order constellations. We experimentally validate our method on both discrete-component and integrated photonic platforms, demonstrating that a quadrature amplitude modulation format with 256 constellation points can asymptotically approach the Gaussian capacity limit. Beyond quantum key distribution, the principle of tightening uncertainty-constrained bounds via source-mode expansion offers a paradigm for exploring the information-theoretic properties of complex non-Gaussian systems.
one_liner: A security framework for discrete-modulated CV-QKD avoids SDP and links constellation geometry to key rate.
why_it_matters: It reduces a major analysis bottleneck for hardware-realistic CV-QKD and supports high-order modulation on integrated photonic systems.
detailed_summary: The authors replace semidefinite-programming-based security analysis with a framework grounded in the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. A multi-mode entanglement-source model captures non-Gaussian state preparation and gives an explicit relation between constellation geometry and secret key rate. Experiments on discrete-component and integrated photonic platforms validate the method, including 256-point QAM approaching the Gaussian capacity limit asymptotically.
main_result: The work demonstrates uncertainty-principle-based security analysis for high-order discrete-modulated CV-QKD on both bulk and integrated photonic platforms.
application_angle: This helps make CV-QKD more compatible with practical high-speed optical communication hardware and scalable quantum networks.

title: Graviton-induced which-path decoherence in matter-wave interferometry
abstract: We derive which-path decoherence for matter-wave interferometry that arises from tracing out the gravitons of linearized quantum gravity. Because the gravitons are driven linearly by the matter source, the branch-dependent evolution can be solved exactly, and the reduced coherence is given by the characteristic function of the initial graviton state, evaluated at the difference of the branch-induced field displacements. In vacuum, the decoherence exponent equals half the mean number of gravitons radiated by the difference source. For a smooth Gaussian trajectory, it reduces to $Γ_{\rm vac}=(8/15)\,Gm^2d^4/(\hbar c^5τ^4)$, ranging from $10^{-89}$ to $10^{-61}$ across representative matter-wave platforms. For a general squeezed graviton vacuum, we obtain an exact expression in which squeezing either suppresses or enhances the vacuum response, depending on the squeezing phase. For the strongly squeezed state produced by inflation, this expression reduces to $Γ_{\rm inf}=(π/20)\,Ω_{\rm inf}(md^2H_0/\hbar)^2$ and reaches at most $\sim10^{-27}$ for optimistic parameters. Hence, the which-path decoherence induced by radiative gravitons is therefore negligible in current matter-wave interferometers.
one_liner: Radiative gravitons induce vanishingly small which-path decoherence in realistic matter-wave interferometers.
why_it_matters: The calculation bounds a proposed quantum-gravity decoherence channel and shows it is negligible for current interferometric platforms.
detailed_summary: The paper derives matter-wave which-path decoherence by tracing out gravitons in linearized quantum gravity, using exact branch-dependent field displacements. In vacuum, the decoherence exponent equals half the mean graviton number radiated by the difference source and is estimated between 10^-89 and 10^-61 for representative platforms. For squeezed graviton states, including inflationary squeezing, the effect can be enhanced or suppressed but remains tiny, at most about 10^-27 under optimistic parameters.
main_result: The authors show that graviton-induced which-path decoherence is far below detectability in present matter-wave interferometry.
application_angle: It sets practical sensitivity expectations for interferometric probes of quantum-gravity-induced decoherence.

title: Heralded high-dimensional module-based quantum computation
abstract: Parity measurements have been explored as building blocks for preparing and discriminating entangled states, as well as for implementing quantum computation. We first develop two alternative high-dimensional generalized parity modules, and then propose a procedure for constructing high-dimensional generalized module-based controlled-NOT gate. The construction of module-based quantum computing introduced here is deterministic, heralded, insensitive to the dimensionality of the computing basis, and postselection technique is not required. The result shows that out of $(d-1)!$ generalized parity modules, only modules $ \mathcal{P}=(j\ominus i)\bmod d$ and $ \mathcal{P}=(j \oplus i)\bmod d$ can be used as building blocks for high-dimensional quantum computing. Furthermore, we proposed an optical nondestructive scheme for implementing generalized parity module through quantum nondemolition measurements, and the success of the parity module is heralded by photon-number-resolving detectors and single-photon detectors.
one_liner: Proposes heralded high-dimensional optical parity modules for deterministic module-based qudit CNOT construction without postselection.
why_it_matters: High-dimensional photonic logic can raise information density, but practical qudit gates need heralded, scalable primitives that avoid postselection losses.
detailed_summary: The paper develops two generalized parity-module constructions and identifies the only two parity relations suitable as universal building blocks for high-dimensional module-based computation. It then uses these modules to construct a generalized qudit controlled-NOT gate that is deterministic, heralded, and independent of basis dimension. An optical nondestructive implementation is proposed using quantum nondemolition measurements, photon-number-resolving detectors, and single-photon detectors for heralding.
main_result: A heralded, postselection-free scheme for high-dimensional module-based CNOT gates is constructed from specific generalized parity modules.
application_angle: The approach targets scalable photonic quantum processors where qudit encoding and heralded gate operation can improve resource efficiency.

title: Multicritical dissipative phase transitions manipulated by dipole--dipole interactions
abstract: Precise control of criticality in superradiant phase transitions is essential for quantum state engineering and the simulation of nonequilibrium phase transitions. Here, we investigate theoretically multicritical phenomena in a dissipative two-Rydberg-atom cavity--QED system. The intrinisic dipole--dipole interaction between the two Rydberg atoms restructures the energy-level landscape of the atomic subsystem, thereby significantly modifying the boundary of the continuous second-order superradiant phase transition, and shifting both the phase boundary and the multicritical point toward weaker atom--cavity strengths. For sufficiently strong dipole--dipole interactions, the continuous second-order phase transition and the multicritical point both disappear, leaving only a discontinuous first--order phase transition that enables the emergence of a superradiant phase even at arbitrarily weak atom--cavity coupling. This work is of fundamental interest for studying dissipative quantum phase transitions, with potential implications for quantum precision measurement and quantum sensing.
one_liner: Shows how Rydberg dipole-dipole interactions tune multicritical dissipative superradiant phase transitions in a two-atom cavity-QED system.
why_it_matters: Controllable dissipative criticality is a useful resource for quantum state engineering, simulation, and potentially enhanced sensing near phase transitions.
detailed_summary: This theoretical work studies a dissipative cavity-QED system containing two interacting Rydberg atoms. Intrinsic dipole-dipole interactions reshape the atomic energy structure, shifting the second-order superradiant transition boundary and the multicritical point toward weaker atom-cavity coupling. At stronger interaction, the continuous transition and multicritical point vanish, leaving a first-order transition that can support a superradiant phase even at arbitrarily weak coupling.
main_result: Dipole-dipole interactions are shown to control whether the dissipative superradiant transition is continuous, multicritical, or purely first order.
application_angle: The tunable critical landscape could inform cavity-based quantum simulators and sensing protocols that exploit critical response.

title: Measurement of the reduced dipole matrix element in Ba$^+$
abstract: We present a high-precision measurement of the reduced electric-dipole matrix element $\langle P_{1/2}\|r\|S_{1/2}\rangle$ in $^{138}\mathrm{Ba}^+$. By comparing off-resonant scattering rates with dispersive Stark-shift measurements, we determine the matrix element to be $3.322\,7(12)$, corresponding to a $P_{1/2}$ excited-state radiative lifetime of $7.866\,3(56)$~ns. Combining our experimental results with a prior model for the differential scalar polarizability $Δα_0(ω)$, we extract the static value $Δα_0(0) = -73.09(12)$a.u. This determination directly improves the evaluation of the blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, minimizing a prominent systematic limitation in room-temperature $\mathrm{Ba}^+$ optical clock error budgets. These results provide a stringent benchmark for atomic-structure calculations and advance high-precision applications in quantum metrology and tests of fundamental physics.
one_liner: Reports a precision Ba+ dipole matrix element measurement that tightens BBR-shift estimates for Ba+ optical clocks.
why_it_matters: Reducing blackbody-radiation shift uncertainty directly improves room-temperature trapped-ion clock accuracy and benchmarks atomic-structure theory.
detailed_summary: The authors measure the reduced electric-dipole matrix element for the 138Ba+ P1/2-S1/2 transition by comparing off-resonant scattering rates with dispersive Stark-shift data. They obtain a matrix element of 3.3227(12), corresponding to a P1/2 lifetime of 7.8663(56) ns. Combining the result with an existing polarizability model yields a static differential scalar polarizability of -73.09(12) a.u., improving evaluation of the Ba+ clock blackbody-radiation shift.
main_result: The work determines the Ba+ P1/2-S1/2 reduced dipole matrix element and derived polarizability with precision relevant to optical-clock systematics.
application_angle: The result reduces a leading systematic uncertainty for Ba+ optical clocks and supports precision tests of atomic theory and fundamental physics.

title: An Analytically Trained Variational Surrogate for Quantum Phase Estimation on NISQ Hardware
abstract: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is a foundational algorithm for molecular ground-state energy estimation, but its deep circuit requirements make direct hardware execution impractical on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. We present an analytically grounded variational surrogate framework in which a shallow Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) is trained to reproduce the QPE measurement distribution without any quantum circuit simulation. The training target is computed entirely classically via the Dirichlet kernel, evaluated directly from the Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) ground-state energy, the ancilla qubit count, and the time evolution parameter, eliminating the exponentially scaling simulation bottleneck of prior surrogate approaches. We apply this framework to the hydrogen molecule (H$_2$) with a symmetry-tapered Hamiltonian, conducting a four-stage experimental investigation on IBM Quantum hardware. Stage 1 compares linear and full entangler topologies for the $R_Y$-$R_Z$-$CZ$ ansatz, with and without XpXm Dynamical Decoupling (DD), across four distributional metrics (Hellinger distance, fidelity error, total variation distance, Jensen-Shannon divergence), identifying the linear entangler as optimal. Stage 2 varies VQC layers ($p=1$ to $5$) for the linear-entangler ansatz, identifying single-layer depth as optimal under hardware noise. Stage 3 applies this configuration to the reduced $R_Y$-$CZ$ ansatz, comparing ideal and noisy simulator-trained parameters. A supplementary noise analysis at $p \in \{8,64\}$ characterizes the depth-dependent interplay between circuit depth and DD effectiveness. The framework enables faithful QPE mimicry using a linearly scaling VQC, recovering the ground-state energy within the chemical accuracy threshold (1 kcal/mol), constituting a scalable, hardware-efficient paradigm for QPE-based molecular energy estimation on NISQ devices.
one_liner: Demonstrates a shallow variational surrogate for QPE on IBM hardware, reproducing molecular energy estimates within chemical accuracy for H2.
why_it_matters: Replacing deep QPE circuits with trainable shallow surrogates is a practical route to useful molecular energy estimation on noisy quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces an analytically trained variational quantum circuit that mimics the quantum phase estimation measurement distribution without quantum-circuit simulation. The classical training target is computed from the Dirichlet kernel using the FCI ground-state energy, ancilla count, and evolution time. On IBM Quantum hardware for symmetry-tapered H2, the study compares ansatz entanglers, dynamical decoupling, layer counts, and reduced gates, finding a shallow linear-entangler configuration most robust under noise.
main_result: A linearly scaling shallow VQC surrogate reproduces QPE-like H2 energy estimation within the 1 kcal/mol chemical-accuracy threshold.
application_angle: The method offers a hardware-efficient path for near-term molecular energy workflows that would otherwise require circuits too deep for NISQ devices.

title: Monolithic Magneto-Optical Mach-Zehnder Isolator Using Laser-Annealed Iron Garnet on a Silicon Waveguide
abstract: Stable silicon photonic circuits require monolithically integrated optical isolators based on magneto-optical garnet. However, crystallizing the garnet by conventional furnace annealing exposes the entire chip to high temperature and degrades the silicon waveguides and the metal electrodes. Here we avoid this degradation by using local laser annealing in vacuum to crystallize cerium-substituted yttrium iron garnet (Ce:YIG), deposited by ion beam sputtering without a seed layer, directly within a silicon-based Mach-Zehnder interferometer. A 915 nm beam heats only the garnet region confined in micrometer-scale trenches, leaving the surrounding circuit and electrodes intact. The device achieves an isolation ratio of 13.6 dB at a wavelength of 1540 nm, corresponding to a Faraday rotation of 0.092$°$/$μ$m, with an insertion loss of 20.4 dB and a propagation loss of 9.5 dB. Transmission electron microscopy reveals the crystallized Ce:YIG and a ~10 nm boundary region at the interface with the Si waveguide. These results demonstrate that thermally sensitive silicon photonic devices and magneto-optical thin films requiring high-temperature processing can be integrated by a high-throughput technique compatible with mass production.
one_liner: Demonstrates a monolithic silicon Mach-Zehnder optical isolator using laser-annealed Ce:YIG integrated directly on waveguides.
why_it_matters: On-chip optical isolation is a key missing function for stable silicon photonic systems, especially where back-reflections disrupt lasers and quantum circuits.
detailed_summary: The authors integrate cerium-substituted yttrium iron garnet directly into a silicon Mach-Zehnder interferometer by local 915 nm laser annealing in vacuum. This selectively crystallizes the garnet in micrometer-scale trenches while avoiding thermal damage to surrounding waveguides and metal electrodes. The device achieves 13.6 dB isolation at 1540 nm, 0.092 deg/um Faraday rotation, 20.4 dB insertion loss, and 9.5 dB propagation loss, with TEM confirming the crystallized Ce:YIG and interfacial boundary region.
main_result: A monolithically integrated magneto-optical silicon photonic isolator is fabricated using local laser annealing and achieves 13.6 dB isolation.
application_angle: The process is compatible with thermally sensitive photonic circuits and points toward manufacturable nonreciprocal components for integrated optics.

title: Compact deterministic liquid-crystal polarization controller with single-measurement direct control
abstract: Polarization controllers (PCs) and their control algorithms are critical for compensating environmental disturbances and maintaining signal fidelity in polarization-sensitive photonic systems. However, existing controllers often involve trade-offs among key performance metrics, while associated control algorithms either converge inefficiently or require multiple state-of-polarization (SOP) measurements. This work presents a compact deterministic liquid-crystal polarization controller (LC-PC) with balanced overall performance, featuring low insertion loss (<1 dB), low driving voltage (<6 V), and full Poincaré sphere coverage. The device exhibits highly predictable and repeatable polarization modulation characterized by SOP-independent trajectory normal vectors, enabling a single-measurement direct-calculation algorithm with an angular error below 2°. The combination of this compact deterministic LC-PC and its efficient control scheme provides a practical solution for polarization management in quantum key distribution, optical sensing, and advanced photonic systems.
one_liner: Introduces a compact liquid-crystal polarization controller with full Poincare coverage and single-measurement direct control.
why_it_matters: Fast, low-loss, deterministic polarization stabilization is critical for fielded QKD links, optical sensing, and polarization-sensitive photonic systems.
detailed_summary: This work presents a deterministic liquid-crystal polarization controller with insertion loss below 1 dB, driving voltage below 6 V, and full Poincare-sphere coverage. Its polarization trajectories have SOP-independent normal vectors, enabling a direct-calculation control algorithm from a single state-of-polarization measurement. The reported angular error is below 2 degrees, combining compact hardware with efficient feedback-free correction.
main_result: The device provides full-sphere polarization control with low loss, low voltage, repeatable modulation, and single-measurement angular correction below 2 degrees.
application_angle: It is directly relevant to deployed quantum key distribution, fiber photonic links, and optical sensors needing robust polarization management.

title: A Quantum Interface Between Neutral-Atoms and Trapped-Ions Quantum Registers
abstract: Hybrid quantum systems combining neutral atoms and trapped ions offer the prospect of integrating the scalability of atom arrays with the high-fidelity control available in trapped-ion platforms. Here we propose and analyze a quantum interface between individually trapped neutral atoms and a trapped-ion crystal. In our scheme, a neutral 88Sr atom trapped in optical tweezers interacts with a small 88Sr+ ion crystal, and by exciting the atom to a Rydberg state, the atom-ion polarization interaction is strongly enhanced, resulting in a state-dependent modification of the ions' collective motional modes. We show that this shift enables conditional control of a MS gate, allowing the neutral atom to act as a control qubit for an entangling operation between two ions. We investigate the feasibility of the scheme by analyzing Rydberg trapping in the combined optical tweezers and Paul trap potentials, identifying negative-polarizability Rydberg states as particularly favorable for stable confinement. We further evaluate the relevant trapping conditions, Rydberg lifetimes, and coherence requirements, and show that the proposed interface is compatible with realistic experimental parameters. These results establish a practical route toward deterministic atom-ion hybrid quantum gates and quantum interfaces.
one_liner: Proposes a deterministic quantum gate interface linking neutral-atom and trapped-ion registers via Rydberg-enhanced atom-ion coupling.
why_it_matters: A workable atom-ion gate would combine scalable neutral-atom arrays with high-fidelity trapped-ion logic in modular quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The work analyzes a hybrid interface where an optically tweezer-trapped neutral 88Sr atom couples to a small 88Sr+ ion crystal. Exciting the atom to a Rydberg state enhances the atom-ion polarization interaction, shifting the ions' collective motional modes in a qubit-state-dependent way. That shift can conditionally control an ion-ion Mølmer-Sørensen entangling gate, with trapping, lifetime, and coherence estimates checked against realistic parameters.
main_result: The paper shows that a neutral Rydberg atom can act as a control qubit for a two-ion entangling gate under experimentally plausible conditions.
application_angle: It points toward modular quantum computers that use neutral atoms for scale and trapped ions for precise register operations.

title: Structured Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics
abstract: A cavity quantum electrodynamics (cQED) system consisting of a confined single photon and a single quantum emitter serves as a fundamental block for quantum optics and photonic quantum technologies. The canonical optical mode employed in the conventional cavity quantum electrodynamics features a uniform polarization distribution, leading to the scalar light-matter interaction in most existing experiments. Despite the rapid progress in the generation of structured light with spatially varied polarizations, the structured light-matter interaction, especially at the single quanta level, is highly intriguing yet largely unexplored. Here, we present the structured light-matter interaction at the single-photon level in a semiconductor cavity quantum electrodynamics system. Four distinct structured cavity modes that are spectrally close to each other are constructed in a micropillar cavity. By spatially locating a single epitaxial quantum dot (QD) at the periphery of a semiconductor micropillar cavity and spectrally tuning the QD emission wavelength into the resonances of the structured cavity modes, cavity-enhanced single-photon emissions with spin-locked chiral orbital angular momentum (OAM) and engineerable spin-orbit entanglements are achieved within a single wavelength-scale device. Our work opens an unexplored paradigm of structured quantum light-matter interactions and may further advance chiral quantum optics and high-dimensional photonic quantum technology.
one_liner: Demonstrates single-photon structured light-matter coupling in a quantum-dot micropillar cavity with chiral OAM modes.
why_it_matters: It adds spatial polarization and spin-orbit structure as controllable resources inside compact semiconductor quantum photonic devices.
detailed_summary: The paper realizes structured cavity QED using a single epitaxial quantum dot placed near the edge of a semiconductor micropillar cavity. Four spectrally close structured cavity modes provide spatially varying polarization rather than the usual scalar cavity mode. By tuning the dot emission into these modes, the device produces cavity-enhanced single photons with spin-locked chiral orbital angular momentum and engineerable spin-orbit entanglement.
platform_or_system: quantum dot in semiconductor micropillar cavity
main_result: The authors demonstrate structured single-photon light-matter interaction with chiral OAM and tunable spin-orbit correlations in a wavelength-scale cavity.
application_angle: The platform is relevant for integrated chiral quantum optics and high-dimensional photonic encoding.

title: Picosecond-resolved entanglement distribution over an urban free-space channel
abstract: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. In this context, accurate timing is not merely a technical detail, but a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing and exploiting the underlying quantum correlations. Here, we demonstrate the faithful distribution of a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in the center of Rome. The developed system incorporates a synchronization device capable of achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy between the two ends of the link while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.
one_liner: Distributes fast time-evolving entanglement across a 270 m urban free-space link with sub-50 ps synchronization.
why_it_matters: Picosecond timing makes dynamic entangled states usable outside the lab, including noisy city links and future satellite quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The experiment transmits a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel between buildings in central Rome. The system includes synchronization hardware reaching below 50 ps timing accuracy while also supporting channel stabilization. The result shows that time-dependent quantum correlations can be faithfully recovered despite urban atmospheric and alignment noise.
main_result: The team demonstrates reliable distribution and measurement of picosecond-scale evolving entanglement over a 270 m city free-space channel.
application_angle: This is a benchmark for timing-critical quantum communication, clock synchronization, and satellite-style entanglement links.

title: Reassessment of line profile asymmetry in measurements of the 1s-2s energy interval in hydrogen
abstract: Experiments to determine transition frequencies in the hydrogen atom represent some of the most precise spectroscopic measurements and are at a higher level among simple atomic systems. The most persistent measured value in hydrogen is the energy interval corresponding to the $1s-2s$ two-photon transition. The achieved experimental precision is several parts of $10^{-15}$ and has not changed over the last two decades. Although repeated experiments in 2011 and 2013 have improved the accuracy by several times, the frequency value has not changed significantly. On this basis, the frequency of the $1s-2s$ transition holds pivotal for determining physical quantities such as the Rydberg constant and the proton charge radius. Theoretical efforts to study in detail the effects that might influence such precise measurements have not revealed significant contributions. The present work revises the theoretical analysis of the line contour asymmetry and its influence on the determination of the two-photon absorption transition frequency, taking into account the theoretical achievements of recent years in this direction. It is shown that the asymmetry of the observed profile can lead to a $1s-2s$ transition frequency shift at the level of modern experimental accuracy. The found frequency shift is consistent with the line shape model contribution that forms the error budget of the experimental measurements. Adjustment can be carried out on the basis of the asymmetric profile that has become standard in recent years.
one_liner: Reassesses hydrogen 1s-2s line-shape asymmetry and finds shifts at the level of modern spectroscopic accuracy.
why_it_matters: Hydrogen spectroscopy anchors constants such as the Rydberg constant and proton radius, so line-shape systematics directly affect precision metrology.
detailed_summary: The paper revisits theoretical treatment of asymmetric line profiles in two-photon 1s-2s hydrogen spectroscopy. It argues that profile asymmetry can shift the inferred transition frequency at the level relevant to current experimental accuracy. The calculated effect is consistent with the line-shape model contribution already used in experimental error budgets and supports adjustment using modern asymmetric profiles.
main_result: The analysis identifies a line-profile asymmetry shift large enough to matter for state-of-the-art hydrogen 1s-2s frequency measurements.
application_angle: Improved control of this systematic supports more reliable fundamental-constant extraction and precision atomic metrology.

title: Conditional probabilities in quantum-optical settings
abstract: We examine conditional probabilities derived from the joint noisy measurement of two complementary observables. We show that conditioning on one variable can lead to reduction of uncertainty in the other one, even completely eliminating uncertainty. We show that the conditional distribution cannot, in general, be represented in Born form using the marginal positive operator valued measure and any physical system state, nor can it be derived from typical rules of state reduction. We examine these issues in two basic quantum-optical schemes. These are double homodyne detection and a qubit measurement.
one_liner: Analyzes conditional probabilities from noisy joint measurements in quantum-optical systems and their non-Born-form behavior.
why_it_matters: Clarifying conditioning under joint optical measurements matters for interpreting uncertainty, state update rules, and measurement-based protocols.
detailed_summary: The paper studies conditional distributions obtained from joint noisy measurements of complementary observables. It shows that conditioning on one outcome can reduce, or even eliminate, uncertainty in the other variable. However, these conditional distributions generally cannot be represented as Born probabilities using the marginal POVM and any physical state, nor derived from standard state-reduction rules, as illustrated in double homodyne and qubit measurement settings.
platform_or_system: double homodyne and qubit optical measurement schemes
main_result: The work demonstrates that operational conditional probabilities in noisy joint measurements can violate simple Born-form or state-update interpretations.
application_angle: The results sharpen modeling of quantum-optical measurement data used in communication, sensing, and measurement-based information processing.

title: Duality constrains optimal thresholds in quantum error correction
abstract: Error correction thresholds are often treated as the primary figure of merit for comparing quantum error-correcting code families. We show that the optimal error correction threshold for many commonly considered codes is constrained to a single universal value at leading order in a replica limit. Through a statistical mechanical mapping, we demonstrate that duality constrains all zero-rate em-symmetric CSS codes to have the same optimal code capacity threshold. Here, em symmetry means that the X- and Z-type parity-check matrices are equivalent up to row and column permutations. Under this statistical mechanical mapping, em-symmetric CSS codes are self-dual under a generalized Kramers-Wannier duality up to a mixing of logical sectors. For zero-rate code families, this mixing contributes only subextensive corrections, so the thermodynamic bulk free energy is self-dual in the trivial logical sector. This self-duality fixes the clean critical point and constrains the disordered phase boundary. We also show that self-duality is preserved under code concatenation, and that optimal decoding of concatenated codes can be reformulated as a renormalization group flow on a hierarchical lattice. Our results provide a common framework for analyzing topological, concatenated, and more general quantum low-density parity-check code families, including both their optimal code capacity thresholds and their sub-threshold logical error suppression.
one_liner: Shows duality fixes leading-order optimal thresholds for broad classes of zero-rate em-symmetric CSS quantum codes.
why_it_matters: A universal threshold constraint reframes how hardware-relevant quantum error-correcting codes should be compared and optimized.
detailed_summary: The paper maps zero-rate em-symmetric CSS codes to statistical-mechanical models and shows they are self-dual under a generalized Kramers-Wannier duality, up to logical-sector mixing. In the zero-rate limit, that mixing contributes only subextensive corrections, forcing the thermodynamic bulk free energy to be self-dual in the trivial sector.
