The same framework covers topological, concatenated, and more general quantum LDPC families, with concatenated decoding viewed as a renormalization-group flow on a hierarchical lattice.
main_result: The authors derive a universal leading-order constraint on optimal code-capacity thresholds for many zero-rate self-dual CSS code families.
application_angle: The framework can guide realistic code selection and decoder benchmarking for fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Basis-independent coherence and quantum correlations in two dipole-dipole-coupled electrons in double quantum-dot molecules
abstract: This work examines the thermal dynamics of basis-independent quantum coherence and correlation-based quantum resources for two dipole-dipole-coupled electrons confined in spatially separated quantum-dot (QD) molecules. Single-dot quantum superpositions and inter-subsystem coherence are characterized by using localized and collective coherence. Quantum correlations between the two double quantum dots are quantified by employing Bures distance entanglement, Local quantum uncertainty (LQU), and local quantum Fisher Information (LQFI). The findings show that dipole-dipole coupling $K$ is the most effective protective parameter, extending the entanglement sudden death temperature, diminishing the local quantum superpositions and enhancing the collective coherence. The dipole-dipole interaction has also a crucial impact on protecting LQU and LQFI beyond the entanglement sudden death temperature. Coulomb repulsion $J$ reinforces this protection through an independent channel, projecting the thermal state onto the entangled $\{|0_A 1_B\rangle,|1_A 0_B\rangle\}$ subspace; their combined action is required to approach the entanglement maximum, and it enhances collective coherence and extends the temperature range over which LQU and LQFI remain appreciable. Energy detuning $\varepsilon$ can enhance localized coherence but paradoxically accelerates the entanglement sudden death and quenches LQU and LQFI by weakening two-body correlations. Inter-dot tunneling $Γ$ enhances local superpositions at low temperature, but it reduces collective coherence, lowers the entanglement sudden death temperature, and disrupts other nonclassical correlations.
one_liner: Thermal quantum resources are mapped in dipole-coupled double quantum-dot molecules with tunable coupling, detuning, repulsion, and tunneling.
why_it_matters: It identifies which device parameters protect coherence, entanglement, LQU, and LQFI in coupled quantum-dot electron systems at finite temperature.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes two spatially separated double quantum-dot molecules containing dipole-dipole-coupled electrons. It compares localized and collective basis-independent coherence with Bures entanglement, local quantum uncertainty, and local quantum Fisher information under thermal conditions. Dipole coupling and Coulomb repulsion protect nonclassical correlations, while detuning and tunneling can enhance local superposition but degrade two-body quantum resources.
main_result: Dipole-dipole coupling is found to extend entanglement survival temperature and preserve LQU and LQFI beyond entanglement sudden death.
application_angle: The parameter map is relevant for engineering robust semiconductor quantum-dot resources for quantum information processing and sensing protocols.

title: ARGON: A GNN-Empowered Compilation Framework for Scalable Neutral Atom Computing
abstract: Neutral atom quantum systems offer a promising pathway to large-scale quantum computing due to high qubit uniformity and flexible connectivity. To exploit this architecture, compilers must coordinate dynamic atom transport alongside highly parallel entangling gates. As circuits scale, the interplay between these operations becomes a system bottleneck, introducing denser logical interactions and longer temporal dependencies. Compilers must simultaneously satisfy rigid spatial constraints and complex movement schedules. Existing joint spatiotemporal compilation methods face an exponentially expanding search space, incurring substantial overheads or compromising fidelity as circuit size grows. In this work, we propose ARGON, a scalable compilation framework that introduces a spatiotemporal decoupling paradigm for neutral atom processors. Our key novelty is offloading static geometric conflict resolution to an offline phase, precomputing a library of hardware-certified, high-parallelism spatial layouts. To guide temporal routing, we deploy a Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictor to evaluate candidate layouts against deep temporal horizons, proactively evading downstream kinematic bottlenecks. Finally, a heuristic router translates the selected sequence into collision-free physical transport. Evaluations show ARGON completes compilation in under 10 seconds, delivering up to a >10^4x and 600x average speedup over state-of-the-art baselines. ARGON also minimizes routing decoherence and reduces Rydberg stages, improving execution fidelity by up to 10^2x on dense circuits.
one_liner: ARGON uses offline layout certification plus a GNN predictor to compile scalable neutral-atom circuits with fast, collision-free routing.
why_it_matters: Compilation is a practical bottleneck for large neutral-atom processors, and ARGON reports major speedups while improving predicted execution fidelity.
detailed_summary: ARGON decouples neutral-atom compilation into offline spatial layout certification and online temporal routing. A graph neural network scores candidate layouts over long temporal horizons to avoid later transport bottlenecks, and a heuristic router converts the selected sequence into collision-free atom motion. Reported evaluations show sub-10-second compilation, speedups exceeding 10000x in some cases, and up to 100x fidelity improvement on dense circuits.
main_result: The framework compiles large neutral-atom circuits in under 10 seconds while reducing routing decoherence and Rydberg-stage count.
application_angle: It targets scalable operation of neutral-atom quantum computers where atom movement and parallel entangling gates must be scheduled efficiently.

title: Why Some Quantum States Cannot Be Recovered
abstract: The recovery of quantum information after subsystem loss is a central challenge in quantum information processing. However, some states remain beyond the reach of any recovery strategies. Here we identify the algebraic origin of irrecoverability, the ghost information---correlations encoded in the global state that leave no trace on any accessible subsystem. We introduce a scalar measure quantifying its magnitude and prove a universal error floor below which no virtual recovery map can operate, irrespective of resource investment. We further uncover a spectral phase transition in the sampling cost: bounded when the underlying linear map exhibits a spectrum gap, and divergent with a universal exponent in the gapless regime. Together with the universal error floor, this dichotomy organizes all multipartite quantum states into four classes. Moreover, it is revealed that conditional mutual information---the standard entropic diagnostic---is fundamentally irrelevant to virtual recoverability. As an implication, we show that the error floor imposes a detection threshold for loss-tolerant quantum metrology.
one_liner: The work defines ghost information as a source of irrecoverability and derives an unavoidable error floor for virtual recovery.
why_it_matters: It gives a formal limit on when lost quantum information cannot be recovered, with direct implications for loss-tolerant metrology thresholds.
detailed_summary: The paper identifies global correlations that leave no signature on accessible subsystems as ghost information. It introduces a scalar measure of this hidden information and proves a universal lower bound on virtual recovery error, independent of resources. The authors also find a spectral transition in sampling cost and argue that conditional mutual information is not the relevant diagnostic for virtual recoverability.
platform_or_system: multipartite quantum states under subsystem loss
main_result: A universal recovery error floor is derived from ghost information, alongside a gap-dependent sampling-cost phase transition.
application_angle: For quantum sensing, the result sets a detection threshold below which loss-tolerant metrological recovery cannot succeed.

title: Space-division multiplexed quantum key distribution exploiting multi-plane light conversion for few-mode fibers
abstract: As quantum key distribution (QKD) progresses from laboratory demonstrations toward practical deployment, quantum communi- cation networks increasingly require higher key rates and the ability to distribute independent secret keys among multiple users and network nodes. In this paper we present a promsing approach with multi-plane light conversion (MPLC) for demultiplexing entangled photons, transmitted through a few-mode fiber (FMF). We experimentally demonstrated a spatially multiplexed BBM92 QKD scheme. The modes are selectively excited through separate single-mode-fibers and subsequently separated by MPLC into distinct output ports. Unlike high-dimensional QKD based on coherent modal superpositions, our approach exploits distinguishable guided modes as parallel channels while preserving the entanglement required for QKD. For the multiplexed links, we obtain quantum bit error rates of $1.9 \pm 0.4\%$ for the channel 1 and $6.8 \pm 0.8\%$ for the channel 2. These results are relevant for scalable quantum-secured networks, space-division-multiplexed QKD systems, multi-user entanglement distribution, and future quantum internet architectures, where parallel quantum channels must be implemented without compromising the quantum correlations required for security.
one_liner: Entangled-photon BBM92 QKD is spatially multiplexed through few-mode fiber using MPLC demultiplexing into parallel modal channels.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates a route to higher-capacity QKD links by carrying independent entangled channels without relying on fragile modal superpositions.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses multi-plane light conversion to separate distinguishable guided modes transmitted through a few-mode fiber. Separate single-mode inputs selectively excite modes that are demultiplexed into different output ports while preserving entanglement for BBM92 QKD. The multiplexed channels achieve quantum bit error rates of 1.9 ± 0.4% and 6.8 ± 0.8%.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrate spatially multiplexed entanglement-based BBM92 QKD over two few-mode-fiber channels.
application_angle: The approach is relevant for scalable quantum-secured networks, multi-user entanglement distribution, and higher-throughput quantum internet links.

title: Classifying Topology via Edge-State Pure Thermalization
abstract: Repeated-interaction machines distinguish heat-like from work-like resources through the steady states they generate, but whether topology can control this distinction remains unknown. Here we reveal the role of topology in the process by showing that topological edge states can act as pure-thermalization fuels. For an open Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain used as the fuel source of a micromaser, edge eigenstates suppress both displacement and squeezing and drive the cavity to a Gibbs state, whereas bulk eigenstates activate coherent channels and yield thermo-mechanical operation. This edge-bulk thermodynamic dichotomy remains robust under realistic decoherence, cavity loss, bond disorder, and moderate onsite disorder. We further design a superconducting implementation in which a sixteen-site SSH eigenstate is deterministically compressed into a four-qubit fuel register. The resulting cavity response provides a transport-free classifier of topology and identifies a topology-thermodynamics link that extends beyond cavity-QED to repeated-interaction settings more generally.
one_liner: Topological SSH edge states are shown to drive pure thermalization in a micromaser while bulk states activate coherent work-like channels.
why_it_matters: It links topology to operational thermodynamics and proposes a cavity-response classifier that avoids transport measurements.
detailed_summary: The paper studies an open Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain used as a fuel source for a micromaser. Edge eigenstates suppress cavity displacement and squeezing, yielding a Gibbs state, while bulk eigenstates generate coherent thermo-mechanical operation. The edge-bulk contrast is reported robust to decoherence, cavity loss, bond disorder, and moderate onsite disorder, with a proposed superconducting circuit implementation compressing a 16-site SSH eigenstate into four qubits.
main_result: Topological edge states produce pure thermalization signatures distinct from bulk-state coherent cavity responses.
application_angle: The cavity response offers a practical, transport-free method to classify topology in photonic or superconducting repeated-interaction platforms.

title: Quasiparticle-induced transitions in a fluxonium qubit
abstract: Quasiparticles are a prominent decoherence source in superconducting qubits, but their effects are notoriously difficult to isolate in fluxonium. Unlike a transmon, fluxonium is insensitive to offset charge, precluding charge-parity detection of quasiparticle tunneling. We address this challenge by measuring the excitation and de-excitation rates in a fluxonium qubit under controlled on-chip quasiparticle injection. We show that to accurately model the external magnetic flux dependence of the quasiparticle-induced transition rates, it is necessary to account for the superconducting gap asymmetry across the Josephson junctions. A comparison between theory and experiment constrains the relative quasiparticle contributions of the junction array and the small junction and helps explain previously reported discrepancies between the bounds on the quasiparticle densities inferred for these two circuit elements.
one_liner: Controlled quasiparticle injection is used to measure flux-dependent excitation and relaxation rates in a fluxonium qubit.
why_it_matters: It isolates a key superconducting-qubit decoherence channel and improves modeling of quasiparticle effects in fluxonium hardware.
detailed_summary: The study measures excitation and de-excitation rates in a fluxonium qubit while injecting quasiparticles on chip. Because fluxonium lacks transmon-like charge-parity sensitivity, the experiment uses transition-rate spectroscopy to identify quasiparticle effects. Agreement with flux-dependent data requires superconducting gap asymmetry across Josephson junctions, constraining contributions from the junction array and small junction.
main_result: The authors quantify quasiparticle-induced transition rates and show that junction gap asymmetry is needed to model their flux dependence.
application_angle: The measurements inform decoherence budgets and materials or circuit design strategies for higher-coherence superconducting quantum processors.

title: Floquet Reservoir Engineering for Remote Logical Entanglement
abstract: Implementing controlled dissipative dynamics is a powerful approach for state preparation in a variety of contexts, including the preparation of remote entangled states. Here, we show that by going beyond the standard setting of time-independent dissipative dynamics, one can realize even more powerful non-unitary protocols. We introduce dissipative Floquet protocols for stabilizing remote entanglement of logical qubits, where continuously-running dissipation is interleaved with a periodic sequence of unitary gates. These protocols harness existing experimental capabilities, and overcome time-entanglement limits that constrain standard approaches. They also implement an autonomous form of entanglement distillation. We show how these protocols give enhanced protection against waveguide loss, and as an example, analyze a specific implementation using cat-qubits and transmons in a superconducting circuit.
one_liner: Dissipative Floquet protocols stabilize remote logical entanglement beyond steady-state reservoir-engineering limits.
why_it_matters: Time-periodic gates plus dissipation could make autonomous entanglement generation and distillation more robust to channel loss in modular quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes remote logical-entanglement stabilization using continuously running dissipation interleaved with periodic unitary gate sequences. This Floquet reservoir-engineering approach relaxes time-entanglement constraints of time-independent dissipative protocols and implements autonomous entanglement distillation. A superconducting-circuit implementation with cat qubits and transmons is analyzed, including enhanced tolerance to waveguide loss.
main_result: The authors show that dissipative Floquet protocols can stabilize and distill remote logical entanglement with improved protection against waveguide loss.
application_angle: The approach targets modular fault-tolerant hardware where remote logical links must be generated autonomously and robustly.

title: QuantumChain: Blockchain-Backed Quantum Federated Learning for Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Financial fraud detection is challenged by decentralized data, severe class imbalance, and privacy constraints. This paper presents QuantumChain, a secure Quantum Federated Learning (QFL) framework that combines hybrid quantum-classical neural networks, encrypted federated aggregation, blockchain-based auditability, and quantum-secure communication. Each client trains a local hybrid model in which a variational quantum circuit is embedded between classical neural layers, while model updates are protected through homomorphic encryption, threshold secret sharing, and QKD-based keying. A permissioned blockchain records aggregation events and supports reputation-weighted trust among participants. We evaluate QuantumChain on financial transaction data using a compact, size-matched classical baseline to isolate the effect of the quantum layer. Results show that the HQNN achieves comparable accuracy while improving fraud-class recall in most settings, reaching 94.6% recall compared with 93.2% for the classical model. The Deep QLayer improves performance in full-data settings, suggesting that added circuit depth helps recover representational capacity when the shallow circuit becomes limited. Mixed-state simulations further show that the recall trend persists under non-ideal quantum evolution. In federated deployment with 10 heterogeneous clients, global accuracy increases from 97.7% to 98.8% over five rounds before stabilizing. These results show that QuantumChain can integrate depth-aware hybrid quantum models into a secure federated fraud-detection pipeline while maintaining stable global convergence.
one_liner: QuantumChain combines hybrid quantum federated learning with encrypted aggregation, blockchain auditability, and QKD keying for fraud detection.
why_it_matters: It explores how hybrid quantum models could be embedded into privacy-preserving, auditable financial ML workflows under federated deployment constraints.
detailed_summary: QuantumChain uses local hybrid quantum-classical neural networks with variational quantum circuits embedded between classical layers. Model updates are protected by homomorphic encryption, threshold secret sharing, and QKD-based keying, while a permissioned blockchain logs aggregation and trust events. The reported experiments show comparable accuracy to a size-matched classical baseline, higher fraud-class recall in most settings, and stable convergence across 10 heterogeneous clients.
main_result: The framework reaches 94.6% fraud recall versus 93.2% for the classical baseline and improves global federated accuracy from 97.7% to 98.8% over five rounds.
application_angle: The system is aimed at privacy-constrained financial fraud detection where institutions cannot pool raw transaction data.

title: Directional telecom photons from a chirally coupled quantum dot
abstract: Chiral quantum light-matter interfaces, where the internal spin state of a quantum emitter determines the direction in which it emits, are essential building blocks of non-reciprocal quantum devices, deterministic quantum logical gates and entanglement generation protocols. Yet, a chiral quantum interface that operates at telecom wavelengths, and is compatible with telecommunication infrastructure and silicon photonics, does not yet exist. Here, we report on an integrated chiral quantum interface in the original telecom band (1260-1360 nm), created by interfacing InAs quantum dots with a waveguide-coupled InP microdisk. We tune the quantum dot transitions through the photonic cavity using a strong magnetic field, observing a peak cavity enhancement of 3.3 and an emission directionality of 0.985, demonstrating the near-ideal chiral quantum coupling required for quantum information processing on integrated photonic devices.
one_liner: An InAs quantum dot coupled to an InP microdisk emits near-directional chiral photons in the telecom O-band.
why_it_matters: A telecom-wavelength chiral emitter compatible with fiber networks and silicon photonics is a key component for scalable nonreciprocal quantum photonic circuits.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates an integrated chiral light-matter interface by coupling InAs quantum dots to a waveguide-coupled InP microdisk operating from 1260 to 1360 nm. A strong magnetic field tunes dot transitions through the cavity, enabling spin-dependent directional emission. The device reaches a peak cavity enhancement of 3.3 and an emission directionality of 0.985.
platform_or_system: InAs quantum dot in InP microdisk
main_result: The experiment demonstrates near-ideal chiral quantum coupling at telecom wavelengths with directionality of 0.985.
application_angle: This advances telecom-compatible building blocks for nonreciprocal devices, deterministic photonic gates, and entanglement distribution.

title: Rack-integrated quantum dot-based source of single and entangled photons at telecom C-band
abstract: For quantum light sources in everyday telecommunication networks, quantum science needs to be fully transformed into quantum technology. The first necessary step to move outside a well-controlled lab environment requires the use of quantum light sources operating in the technologically relevant telecom O- and C-band. This can be provided using epitaxial quantum dots as deterministic sources of quantum light. Particularly intriguing is that emitters operating at telecom wavelengths are rapidly catching up with their short wavelength counterparts in terms of performances. Here, we make a decisive step forward in the development of quantum communication networks: a state-of-the-art source of quantum light, a semiconductor quantum dot (QD), with record coincidence rate for entangled photon emission in the telecom C-band, is operated inside an optimized rack-based setup. This setup includes a tunable pulsed laser for the QD excitation (from quasi- to fully resonant excitation), all optics for the excitation filtering, and QD signal coupling into single-mode fibers. Overall, the setup allows for above $50\%$ transmission for both exciton and biexciton photons. These results show that quantum dots-based telecom light sources can now be transported and integrated into existing fiber infrastructures, an important step to demonstrate the feasibility of the upcoming quantum internet.
one_liner: A rack-integrated telecom C-band quantum-dot source delivers single and entangled photons with high fiber-coupled transmission.
why_it_matters: Moving a high-performance quantum-dot photon source into a rack format is a practical step toward deployable quantum communication infrastructure.
detailed_summary: The paper reports a rack-based semiconductor quantum-dot light source for single and entangled photons in the telecom C-band. The integrated setup includes a tunable pulsed excitation laser, excitation filtering optics, and coupling of exciton and biexciton photons into single-mode fibers. It achieves above 50% transmission for both photon lines and a record coincidence rate for telecom C-band entangled photon emission.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a transportable rack system producing telecom C-band single and entangled photons with above 50% transmission for exciton and biexciton channels.
application_angle: The source is designed for integration with existing fiber networks and field-ready quantum internet demonstrations.

title: An on-chip programmable mechano-quantum transducer
abstract: Solid-state spin defects encode local perturbations as measurable shifts in spin-transition frequencies, but mechanical actuation and quantum readout remain physically separated, resulting in a discrete measurement setup. Integrating these functions requires an on-site mechano-quantum interface that programs the lattice state of a defect host and quantitatively maps it onto the spin Hamiltonian. Here we first report an on-chip programmable mechano-quantum transducer (OCPMQT) that integrates voltage-defined micromechanical actuation with in situ spin-frequency readout in a two-dimensional van der Waals quantum-defect host. Mechanically programmed lattice states are encoded as shifts in the axial zero-field splitting parameter and resolved by optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectroscopy. Within a chip volume of 2.05*10^-2 cm^3, the transducer accesses ODMR-inferred strains as low as 0.0080% and delivers a volumetric force density of approximately 2.6*104 N/m^-3. A micromechanical-to-spin-Hamiltonian framework links on-chip electromechanics, interfacial strain transfer, and strain-spin coupling, enabling the electrical control micromechanical input to be measured directly as spin-frequency response.
one_liner: An on-chip electromechanical device programs strain in a 2D defect host and reads it through ODMR spin-frequency shifts.
why_it_matters: Co-integrating mechanical actuation and quantum readout enables compact programmable strain-to-spin interfaces for sensing and transduction.
detailed_summary: The authors demonstrate an on-chip programmable mechano-quantum transducer that combines voltage-defined micromechanical actuation with in situ ODMR readout in a two-dimensional van der Waals defect host. Programmed lattice states are mapped to axial zero-field-splitting shifts in the spin Hamiltonian. The device resolves ODMR-inferred strains down to 0.0080% in a 2.05e-2 cm^3 chip volume and provides a volumetric force density near 2.6e4 N/m^3.
main_result: The device electrically programs micromechanical strain and directly measures the corresponding spin-frequency response on chip.
application_angle: This could support integrated force, strain, and material-state sensors with electrically programmable local actuation.

title: Experimental realization of a rotating radio-frequency ion trap for precision metrology
abstract: We discuss the experimental realization of the rotating radio-frequency (rrf) trap, proposed by Hasegawa and Bollinger [Phys. Rev. A 72, 043403 (2005)]. Compared to a traditional linear rf (lrf) Paul trap, the rrf trap is a closer analogy to the popular mechanical lecture demonstration for a Paul trap. In an ion trap with reslistic, non-ideal electrode geometry, the rrf trap averages over angular variations in the effective potential. This averaging provides more uniform confinement and reduces ion loss at equal confinement strength compared with the lrf trap. This feature makes the rrf trap configuration advantageous for precision metrology application, such as electron electric dipole moment (eEDM) measurements.
one_liner: A rotating RF ion trap is experimentally realized to average angular potential imperfections and improve confinement uniformity.
why_it_matters: More uniform ion confinement can reduce loss and systematic errors in precision-metrology traps, including eEDM measurement platforms.
detailed_summary: The paper reports an experimental implementation of the rotating radio-frequency trap proposed by Hasegawa and Bollinger. Unlike a linear RF Paul trap, the rotating field averages over angular variations in the effective potential caused by realistic electrode imperfections. The result is more uniform confinement and reduced ion loss at comparable confinement strength, making the architecture attractive for precision metrology.
main_result: The experiment realizes an rrf ion trap and shows that angular averaging improves confinement uniformity and reduces ion loss relative to linear RF operation.
application_angle: The trap geometry is relevant for high-precision ion-based measurements where confinement imperfections limit sensitivity and control.

title: Extended Single-Atom Tweezer Arrays in High-Cooperativity Cavity-QED
abstract: A central challenge for cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is to make high-cooperativity optical interfaces compatible with site-resolved arrays of single atoms. Here, we demonstrate optical tweezer arrays of individual $^{87}$Rb atoms inside a fiber Fabry-Perot microcavity with single-atom cooperativity $\mathcal{C} \sim 90$. We combine background-free site-resolved fluorescence imaging of extended arrays with collective coupling to a common cavity mode for arrays with a mean atom number up to $\bar{N} \simeq 36$. These results establish a high-cooperativity platform for many-body cavity-QED with site-resolved detection and control.
one_liner: Single Rb atoms in extended tweezer arrays are integrated with a high-cooperativity fiber Fabry-Perot cavity.
why_it_matters: It combines scalable site-resolved neutral-atom arrays with a strong optical interface needed for cavity-mediated gates, readout, and many-body QED.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates arrays of individual 87Rb atoms trapped by optical tweezers inside a fiber Fabry-Perot microcavity with single-atom cooperativity near 90. It reports background-free, site-resolved fluorescence imaging of extended arrays while preserving collective coupling to a shared cavity mode. Arrays with mean atom number up to about 36 atoms are coupled to the cavity, establishing a many-atom interface with local detection and control.
platform_or_system: 87Rb tweezer arrays in a fiber Fabry-Perot cavity
main_result: The authors realize site-resolved neutral-atom arrays inside a high-cooperativity cavity and observe collective coupling for arrays up to roughly 36 atoms.
application_angle: The platform is directly relevant to cavity-mediated neutral-atom processors, quantum networks, and controlled many-body light-matter experiments.

title: Strategic Plan for Neutral Atom Quantum Computation
abstract: We present a strategic plan for neutral atom quantum computation, bringing together hardware development and theory advancements to achieve the goal of practical quantum advantage. The concept of practical quantum advantage is defined, along with how to verify claims of advantage, and approaches to designing quantum algorithms that deliver practical advantage. Future directions for neutral atom quantum processor hardware are described: scaling-up system size, Qubit encodings and atomic platforms, going further below threshold with neutral-atom logical-qubit performance, continuous reloading of qubits, and fast readout. We also explore opportunities for scalable integrated photonic control technologies. Alongside hardware advancements, new developments in quantum error correction and compilation of quantum circuits are proposed. Finally, we examine the opportunity of networking multiple neutral atom quantum processors together to perform distributed quantum computing and overcome possible limitations of a single system.
one_liner: A roadmap lays out hardware, algorithms, photonic control, QEC, and networking paths for neutral-atom quantum advantage.
why_it_matters: It synthesizes the main engineering bottlenecks and system-level milestones for turning neutral-atom processors into practical quantum computers.
detailed_summary: The paper defines practical quantum advantage and discusses how such claims could be verified for neutral-atom systems. It outlines hardware directions including larger arrays, improved qubit encodings and atomic species, lower logical error rates, continuous reloading, and faster readout. It also covers integrated photonic control, compilation, quantum error correction, and networking multiple processors for distributed computation.
main_result: The main contribution is a strategic technical plan for scaling neutral-atom quantum computers toward practical quantum advantage.
application_angle: The roadmap is useful for prioritizing hardware, control, QEC, and networking investments in deployable neutral-atom computing systems.

title: Enhancing Entanglement Purification with Shared Randomness
abstract: Entanglement purification protocols (EPPs) are essential for improving entanglement fidelity to support fault-tolerant distributed quantum information processing. Practical entanglement sources are often heterogeneous and source labels may be unavailable at the EPP layer. We show that classical shared randomness, together with buffer memories, can enhance entanglement purification when source labels are unavailable, without state characterization or EPP circuit optimization. The strategy is to accumulate multiple entanglement distribution rounds and then use shared randomness to shuffle all the stored entangled states before packaging them as inputs to the EPP. For any $n$ Werner sources and any fixed $n$-to-1 bilocal Clifford EPP, we prove that accumulating and shuffling improves the expected success probability and the success-weighted output Bell fidelity over the baseline without accumulating and shuffling, for every $n$, for every finite number of accumulation rounds and in the asymptotic limit, and the improvement increases monotonically with the number of accumulation rounds.
one_liner: Shared randomness and memory-buffer shuffling can improve entanglement purification without source labels.
why_it_matters: It offers a low-overhead classical coordination layer that boosts distributed entanglement quality under realistic heterogeneous-source conditions.
detailed_summary: The paper studies entanglement purification when states come from heterogeneous sources but source labels are unavailable to the purification layer. The proposed method accumulates multiple distribution rounds in buffers and uses shared randomness to jointly shuffle stored pairs before feeding them to a fixed n-to-1 bilocal Clifford EPP. For n Werner sources, the authors prove improvements in expected success probability and success-weighted Bell fidelity for finite and asymptotic accumulation, with monotonic gain as accumulation grows.
main_result: The authors prove that accumulate-and-shuffle preprocessing improves purification success and output fidelity for fixed bilocal Clifford EPPs over unlabeled Werner sources.
application_angle: This can improve repeater and distributed-computing links using only shared classical randomness and memory, without full source characterization.

title: Micro-electromechanical photonic integrated memristors
abstract: Programmable optical memristors embedded in photonic integrated circuits (PICs) are emerging as an important technology for high-speed optical storage and in-memory optical computing applications. These devices provide multi-level, non-volatile storage of optical phases that can be interrogated at the speed of light, enabling parallel data readout or energy-efficient multiply-accumulate operations in artificial neural networks. However, there remains several outstanding challenges with existing optical memristor technology including durability, material-induced optical losses, large-scale reconfigurability, or fabrication yield for realistic applications. Here we introduce an analog-programmable photonic memristor based on photonic integrated micro-electromechanical (MEMS) cantilevers produced in a CMOS foundry. The memristor consists of low-loss silicon nitride waveguides, requires no additional back-end materials integration, and is all electrically programmed with electrostatic-piezoelectric forces. We demonstrate up to 5-bit phase storage levels, 50 kbit/s programming speeds, strain-assisted non-volatility lifetimes >1 hour, >1 billion cycle endurance, and stress-tested millions of write-read cycles with pseudorandom bit sequences. We further extend the memory lifetime to several days with simple electronic refresh circuits in a portable battery-powered module, demonstrating a proof-of-concept optical random-access memory in static or dynamic configurations. Our MEMS-photonics technology represents an important step toward practical optical memristors.
one_liner: CMOS-foundry MEMS photonic memristors store analog optical phase states with high endurance and nonvolatile retention.
why_it_matters: The device addresses durability, loss, yield, and integration barriers for practical optical memory and in-memory photonic computing.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce an analog-programmable optical memristor using micro-electromechanical cantilevers integrated with low-loss silicon nitride photonic circuits. The device is electrically programmed through electrostatic-piezoelectric actuation and requires no added backend optical memory materials. Demonstrations include 5-bit phase levels, 50 kbit/s programming, retention beyond 1 hour, endurance beyond 1 billion cycles, and refresh-extended operation for days in a portable module.
platform_or_system: silicon nitride MEMS photonic integrated memristor
main_result: The work demonstrates foundry-compatible MEMS photonic phase memory with multilevel storage, high endurance, and refreshable nonvolatile operation.
application_angle: It supports scalable optical RAM and energy-efficient photonic neural-network accelerators with lower loss and better manufacturability.

title: Mixed-state topological order and error-correction thresholds in non-Abelian codes: rigorous results
abstract: We present a versatile and mathematically rigorous technique for bounding recovery thresholds in topological codes subject to noise. Our method captures the effect of applying an arbitrary (possibly non-Pauli) local noise channel to the code state of a broad class of two-dimensional codes, including surface codes, non-Abelian quantum doubles, and string-net codes. In each case, we prove that for noise strengths up to some explicit constant value, any initially encoded logical information can be recovered to high precision, and that the noise-corrupted state exhibits key hallmarks of mixed-state topological order: long-range entanglement and emergent higher-form symmetries. We also describe how these methods can be adapted to higher dimensions and correlated noise models.
one_liner: Rigorous bounds show recoverability and mixed-state topological order for broad 2D codes under local noise.
why_it_matters: It strengthens the theoretical basis for non-Abelian and topological-code thresholds beyond idealized Pauli-noise assumptions.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a rigorous method for bounding recovery thresholds in topological quantum codes exposed to arbitrary local noise channels, including non-Pauli noise. It applies to surface codes, non-Abelian quantum doubles, and string-net codes. Below explicit noise-strength constants, encoded information remains recoverable with high precision, while the noisy state retains long-range entanglement and emergent higher-form symmetries associated with mixed-state topological order.
main_result: The authors prove explicit low-noise recoverability bounds and persistence of mixed-state topological order across several topological-code families.
application_angle: The results inform fault-tolerant hardware thresholds and decoder assumptions for more realistic noise in topological quantum processors.

title: Resolving topological order crossovers on NISQ hardware
abstract: Topological phases of matter provide a promising route toward robust quantum information processing, but on present-day noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices the experimentally relevant question is whether signatures of topological crossovers remain resolvable under realistic imperfections. Here, we address this question in the Wen--plaquette model through a two-stage strategy on the IBM Quantum hardware. We first use a tractable system to systematically characterize crossover signatures. Using variationally compiled equilibrium and quench-generated states, we resolve crossovers between stabilizer-dominated and trivial or disorder-dominated regimes through local plaquette stabilizers and a Wilson loop, and quantify their robustness against static disorder, deliberately amplified circuit noise, and effective non-Hermitian fields. The quench dynamics further reveal that plaquette-sector signatures remain substantially more stable deep in the strong-stabilizer regime than near the finite-size crossover. Building on the properties established in the small system, we extend the implementation to a physical two-dimensional IBM processor using a layered representative-qubit construction. The resulting lattice-averaged plaquette response exhibits only weak degradation under intentionally amplified local coherent perturbations. Together, these results connect controlled finite-size characterization with a scalable hardware implementation, providing a practical route for preparing and probing topological signatures on near-term quantum processors.
one_liner: IBM hardware experiments resolve topological-order crossover signatures in the Wen-plaquette model under realistic noise.
why_it_matters: It shows that useful topological diagnostics can survive on near-term processors, linking finite-size studies to scalable hardware probes.
detailed_summary: The study uses variationally compiled equilibrium and quench-generated states to probe topological crossovers in the Wen-plaquette model on IBM Quantum hardware. In small systems, local plaquette stabilizers and a Wilson loop resolve transitions between stabilizer-dominated and trivial or disorder-dominated regimes, including tests with static disorder, amplified circuit noise, and effective non-Hermitian fields. The authors then extend to a physical two-dimensional IBM processor with a layered representative-qubit construction and observe lattice-averaged plaquette responses that degrade weakly under amplified coherent perturbations.
main_result: The paper demonstrates hardware-resolved topological crossover signatures and a scalable representative-qubit implementation on a 2D IBM device.
application_angle: It provides practical diagnostics for preparing and testing topological phases on NISQ machines relevant to robust quantum information processing.

title: Electron shuttling as a probe for charge defects
abstract: Silicon spin qubits are a leading platform for scalable quantum computing, but their performance is limited by charge noise, widely attributed to two-level fluctuators (TLFs). The location of individual TLFs is generally unknown, and existing methods to localise them does not scale favourably with device size. Here, we show that electron shuttling turns a single mobile spin into a scanning probe of individual defects. We show that by shuttling a spin over a range of distances and tracking its coherence loss, one can localise defects along the channel and constrain their switching rate and fluctuation amplitude. Because one shuttled electron sweeps an extended region, the approach scales more favourably than previous methods. Our protocol requires no additional hardware and provides a practical route to mapping the charge-defect landscape of large silicon devices, enabling defect-aware calibration and avoidance in shuttling-based architectures.
one_liner: Electron shuttling turns a silicon spin qubit into a mobile probe for locating charge defects along a device channel.
why_it_matters: It offers a hardware-free way to map two-level fluctuators in larger silicon spin-qubit arrays, supporting defect-aware tuning and routing.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes using a shuttled electron spin as a scanning probe of charge defects in silicon qubit devices. By varying shuttling distance and measuring coherence loss, the protocol can infer defect position while constraining switching rates and fluctuation amplitudes. Because one mobile electron samples an extended path, the method scales better than static local probes and needs no added device hardware.
main_result: The authors show that coherence loss during controlled electron shuttling can localize individual charge fluctuators and estimate their noise parameters.
application_angle: The method could guide calibration, layout choices, and defect avoidance in scalable shuttling-based silicon quantum processors.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata from Kramers-Wannier Dualities and Modular Relations
abstract: Recent work has constructed higher-dimensional analogs of non-invertible symmetries similar to 1+1d Kramers-Wannier duality. Although their continuum descriptions often treat purely gravitational topological terms as inessential counterterms, these terms can have an essential lattice manifestation: they distinguish states prepared by finite-depth quantum circuits (FDQCs) from those entangled by nontrivial quantum cellular automata (QCAs). Motivated by this mismatch, we show that QCAs associated with gravitational topological responses arise in several related settings: (1) lattice realizations of projective $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}_N)$ relations generated by topological operations on symmetries; (2) squares of dualities that generalize the relation between fermionization and Kramers-Wannier duality; (3) lattice implementations of QCAs through higher-form gauging; and (4) invertible phases protected by generalized time-reversal symmetries. We derive new projective $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}_N)$ relations whose projective phases are gravitational topological responses constructed from Stiefel-Whitney classes. We furthermore give a general protocol for preparing the associated QCA-entangled states using finite-depth unitary circuits, measurements, and error correction. These results unify the study of gravitational topological responses in field theories, higher dimensional dualities, and quantum cellular automata.
one_liner: The work links lattice dualities, gravitational response terms, and nontrivial quantum cellular automata entanglement.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when lattice states cannot be generated by ordinary finite-depth circuits, informing fault-tolerant state preparation ideas.
detailed_summary: The paper studies quantum cellular automata arising from lattice realizations of generalized Kramers-Wannier dualities and modular relations. It shows that gravitational topological response terms, often treated as continuum counterterms, distinguish finite-depth circuit states from QCA-entangled states on the lattice. The authors derive projective SL(2,Z_N) relations and give a preparation protocol using finite-depth unitaries, measurements, and error correction.
main_result: The main result is a unified construction of QCA-entangled states tied to gravitational topological responses and higher-form gauging operations.
application_angle: The preparation framework is relevant to engineered topological quantum states and measurement-assisted quantum hardware protocols.

title: Deleterious effect of photon-phonon coupling on microcavities in their application as quantum sources
abstract: In quantum systems, the contact with the environment is detrimental to the purity of the state, thus limiting the practical use of entangled sources in quantum information applications. This loss of purity is observed in the form of additional noise in the tomography of the state. We investigate this noise dependence in $Si_3N_4$ micro-cavities, previously used for quantum state generation, and demonstrate that the dependence of this noise on the temperature is compatible with a coupling of the photonic chips to a thermal reservoir. The control of this noise source is a necessary condition for the efficient implementation of these devices as sources of entangled states in quantum networks.
one_liner: Temperature-dependent noise in Si3N4 microcavity quantum sources is traced to photon-phonon coupling with a thermal reservoir.
why_it_matters: Identifying this impurity mechanism is essential for making chip-scale entangled-photon sources reliable in quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The paper investigates excess noise observed in tomography of quantum states generated by silicon nitride microcavities. The measured temperature dependence is consistent with coupling between the photonic chip and a thermal phonon reservoir. This points to photon-phonon coupling as a practical limit on state purity for integrated entangled-photon sources.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that tomography noise in these microcavity sources follows a temperature dependence compatible with thermal photon-phonon coupling.
application_angle: Thermal-noise control becomes a concrete engineering requirement for deploying integrated entangled sources in quantum communication networks.

title: Tunable nonlinear electromechanics at the zero-point motion scale
abstract: Nonlinearity at the scale of zero-point motion opens new possibilities for the control and readout of nanomechanical systems, but achieving this remains a formidable challenge. Here we demonstrate that ultrastrong coupling (USC) between a nanotube mechanical oscillator and a double-quantum-dot electronic two-level system enables a mechanical Kerr (Duffing) nonlinearity at the zero-point motion scale. In the dispersive regime, this large coupling yields a mechanical anharmonicity of $α= 1.4\%$ - three orders of magnitude larger than in previous work - while preserving the predominantly mechanical nature of the lowest energy states. We further demonstrate a purely quadratic cavity-based continuous readout of the mechanical motion. This continuous nonlinear optomechanical readout is enforced by a double-quantum dot symmetry, which can be broken by gate tuning to introduce a large linear transduction. These results establish a tunable USC platform that enables strong mechanical anharmonicity and nonlinear continuous readout at the zero-point motion scale.
one_liner: A nanotube oscillator coupled to a double quantum dot reaches tunable mechanical nonlinearity at the zero-point scale.
why_it_matters: Strong zero-point-scale anharmonicity enables nonlinear control and continuous readout of nanomechanics near the quantum regime.
detailed_summary: The authors demonstrate ultrastrong coupling between a carbon nanotube mechanical oscillator and a double-quantum-dot electronic two-level system. In the dispersive regime, the coupling produces a mechanical Kerr or Duffing anharmonicity of 1.4 percent while keeping the lowest states mostly mechanical. They also show symmetry-protected quadratic cavity readout that can be gate-tuned into strong linear transduction.
platform_or_system: nanotube electromechanical oscillator with double quantum dot
main_result: The work demonstrates a zero-point-scale mechanical anharmonicity three orders of magnitude larger than prior work plus tunable nonlinear readout.
application_angle: The platform could support quantum-limited nanomechanical sensing, nonlinear phononic devices, and hybrid electromechanical quantum interfaces.

title: SSP-QST: Spectral Subspace Purification for Photonic Quantum State Tomography
abstract: Photonic quantum sensing often uses low-rank entangled probes such as Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), Bell, and NOON states. Although these probes are ideally rank-1, practical quantum state tomography (QST) can produce density-matrix estimates with many small finite-shot and noise-induced eigenmodes. This eigenvalue contamination can increase the estimated entropy of the reconstruction and reduce the quantum Fisher information (QFI) available for downstream sensing, while fixed rank-1 purification can discard valid signal modes when real probes acquire additional signal modes. We introduce Spectral Subspace Purification for Quantum State Tomography (SSP-QST), a rank-adaptive post-processing layer for least-squares quantum state tomography (LS-QST). SSP-QST eigendecomposes the least-squares estimate, computes a Weyl-motivated noise floor from the measured spectrum and shot count, removes eigenmodes below this floor, and renormalises the retained subspace. It requires no rank prior, no iterative optimisation, and only one eigendecomposition. In Qiskit Aer simulations, SSP-QST achieves the highest fidelity among the tested non-iterative baselines across the evaluated probe ranks, with a maximum fidelity gain of $+0.584$. It also improves shot efficiency by at least $8\times$ within the tested range. These results show that SSP-QST can make photonic QST more reliable under finite-shot noise while providing a lightweight reconstruction primitive for feedback-oriented quantum sensing pipelines.
one_liner: SSP-QST adaptively removes noise eigenmodes from photonic tomography without assuming a fixed state rank.
why_it_matters: It improves finite-shot photonic state reconstruction and preserves useful signal modes for downstream quantum sensing metrics.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces Spectral Subspace Purification for Quantum State Tomography as a lightweight post-processing layer for least-squares QST. SSP-QST eigendecomposes the reconstructed density matrix, estimates a shot-noise-motivated eigenvalue floor, discards subfloor modes, and renormalizes the retained subspace. Simulations on photonic sensing probes show improved fidelity over tested non-iterative baselines, with reported gains up to 0.584 and at least 8x shot-efficiency improvement in the tested range.
main_result: The method provides rank-adaptive purification that improves simulated tomography fidelity and shot efficiency without iterative optimization or a rank prior.
application_angle: It is practical for feedback-oriented quantum sensing workflows where fast, robust reconstruction of entangled photonic probes is needed.

title: Norm of resonance states in quantum scattering and electromagnetic systems
abstract: Resonance states spatially diverge and are thus not square integrable. Instead, their norm is defined by the biorthogonal scalar product of left and right states. We replace the corresponding volume integral by a convenient boundary integral in piecewise homogeneous systems and apply this procedure to diverse physical settings. For a quantum particle in any number of dimensions we treat hard-wall and piecewise constant potentials. For electromagnetic systems with piecewise homogeneous material properties, we consider three-dimensional and effectively two-dimensional cavities of arbitrary shape. As examples, we treat the spherical scatterer and the circular disk.
one_liner: A boundary-integral formulation simplifies normalization of divergent resonance states in scattering and optical cavities.
why_it_matters: Cleaner resonance normalization supports modeling of open electromagnetic resonators used in photonic devices and sensors.
detailed_summary: The paper addresses the normalization of resonance states, which diverge spatially and are not square integrable. It replaces the usual biorthogonal volume integral with a boundary-integral expression for piecewise homogeneous systems. The treatment covers quantum particles and electromagnetic cavities, including three-dimensional and effectively two-dimensional resonators of arbitrary shape, with spherical and disk examples.
main_result: The authors derive a practical boundary-integral norm for resonance states in piecewise homogeneous quantum and electromagnetic systems.
application_angle: The formulation can make simulations of microcavities, scatterers, and resonant photonic structures more tractable and reliable.

title: Weak Permanent Anti-Concentration for Random Gaussian Matrices in Boson Sampling
abstract: Recent demonstrations of quantum computational advantage have been driven largely by sampling problems. A prominent model, boson sampling, involves sampling from the output distribution of a linear optical network. However, its classical hardness hinges on two plausible yet less-studied conjectures: the average-case hardness of approximating Gaussian permanents, and the permanent anti-concentration conjecture (PACC). The PACC is a purely mathematical assertion regarding the distributional properties of random Gaussian matrices. While the typical magnitude of the permanent has been established for discrete random matrices, the complex Gaussian case, which governs transition amplitudes in linear optical networks, has remained open. Here, we establish a weak anti-concentration bound by upper-bounding the probability that a random Gaussian permanent is superexponentially smaller than its standard deviation. Tightening this bound to an inverse-polynomial fraction would prove the original PACC. As a corollary, we establish the typical magnitude of Gaussian permanents, on par with Tao and Vu's seminal result for Bernoulli matrices. Combined with the Aaronson-Arkhipov framework, our result implies that classically simulating boson sampling to within a superexponentially small total variation distance would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, assuming the remaining conjectures hold.
one_liner: Proves a weak anti-concentration bound for complex Gaussian permanents, tightening the theory behind boson-sampling hardness.
why_it_matters: It strengthens a key mathematical pillar for linear-optical quantum advantage claims, though it remains short of the full inverse-polynomial PACC.
detailed_summary: The paper establishes that the permanent of a random complex Gaussian matrix is unlikely to be superexponentially smaller than its standard deviation. This gives a weak form of the permanent anti-concentration conjecture used in the Aaronson-Arkhipov boson-sampling hardness framework. It also proves a typical-magnitude result for Gaussian permanents analogous to known Bernoulli-matrix results.
main_result: The main result is a weak permanent anti-concentration theorem for random complex Gaussian matrices.
application_angle: The result sharpens the theoretical basis for validating photonic sampling devices as hard-to-simulate quantum processors.

title: Capacitive Loading in Two-dimensional Fluxonium Quantum Processors
abstract: Capacitive loading has emerged as a major obstacle to scaling fluxonium qubits from one-dimensional to highly connected two-dimensional (2D) architectures, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. We derive an analytical relation between the qubit capacitance budget and the achievable capacitive coupling to external circuit elements, identifying the parasitic capacitances of Josephson junctions and Josephson junction arrays as the dominant source of capacitive loading while showing that the qubit-pad geometry can instead be engineered to mitigate it. Building on these insights, we formulate practical design principles and numerically demonstrate ultrafast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates in 2D fluxonium architectures. Our results reveal that capacitive loading does not constitute a fundamental limit for 2D fluxonium quantum processors.
one_liner: Identifies parasitic junction capacitances as the main source of loading in 2D fluxonium and gives design routes around it.
why_it_matters: It addresses a concrete scaling barrier for highly connected fluxonium processors and argues it is engineering-limited rather than fundamental.
detailed_summary: The work derives an analytical relation linking the fluxonium capacitance budget to achievable coupling with external circuit elements. It attributes harmful capacitive loading mainly to parasitic capacitances from Josephson junctions and junction arrays, while showing that pad geometry can be tuned to reduce the problem. Numerical examples then support ultrafast, high-fidelity gates in 2D fluxonium layouts.
main_result: The paper shows that capacitive loading in 2D fluxonium can be mitigated by circuit and layout design rather than imposing a fundamental scaling limit.
application_angle: These design rules support denser superconducting-qubit layouts with stronger connectivity and practical two-qubit gate operation.

title: Maximal Fisher Budget Forces Blind Directions in Bipartite Collective SU(d) Metrology
abstract: For pure two-qudit probes used in a single fixed setting to estimate a common SU(d) transformation, maximal total Fisher sensitivity and full local identifiability are mutually exclusive. We derive exact identities that determine the trace of the quantum Fisher information matrix from two measurable probe properties: exchange symmetry and collective polarization. Every maximizer is exchange symmetric and maximally entangled. Its Fisher matrix has equal sensitivity in every visible direction, while $d(d-1)/2$ generator directions are blind. More generally, weak compatibility, defined by vanishing mean generator commutators, forces at least $\lfloor d/2\rfloor$ blind directions for every pure bipartite probe. A probe-defined antiunitary invariant classifies the complete Fisher spectrum at maximal entanglement, and approaches to the optimum that preserve exchange symmetry have a divergent Holevo cost. The bipartite obstruction is sharp in particle number: for $N\geq 3$, generalized GHZ probes can satisfy weak compatibility, attain the corresponding $N$-partite Fisher trace bound, and retain full local identifiability. Hence, Fisher sensitivity, weak compatibility, identifiability, and attainable precision are distinct resources in quantum metrology with noncommuting generators.
one_liner: Shows that maximal Fisher sensitivity in two-qudit collective SU(d) metrology necessarily creates blind generator directions.
why_it_matters: It clarifies a hard tradeoff between sensitivity, compatibility, and identifiability in multiparameter quantum sensing with noncommuting parameters.
detailed_summary: For pure bipartite probes estimating a shared SU(d) transformation in one fixed setting, the paper proves that maximal total quantum Fisher information conflicts with full local identifiability. Maximizers are exchange symmetric and maximally entangled, with equal visible sensitivity but d(d-1)/2 blind directions. The obstruction is specific to two particles, since N>=3 generalized GHZ probes can retain full local identifiability while attaining the relevant Fisher trace bound.
main_result: The main result is an exact incompatibility between maximal Fisher budget and full identifiability for pure two-qudit collective SU(d) metrology.
application_angle: It informs probe design for quantum sensors that must estimate multiple noncommuting parameters without losing invisible directions.

title: Dark Polaron Theory for High Intensity Laser Cooling
abstract: Conventional laser control schemes for cooling and gate operation of trapped ions are limited to the regime of weak laser intensities and small Lamb-Dicke parameters. To overcome this limitation, we present the concept of dark polarons: spatially extended states of pseudospin polarization that are fully decoupled from a lambda laser configuration. In this picture, all high-order Lamb-Dicke terms collapse into a single linear coupling independent of laser intensity. We apply it to definitively elucidate the reasons behind cooling rate limitations observed in recent experimental implementations of electromagnetically induced transparency with high-intensity lasers.
one_liner: Introduces dark polarons to describe high-intensity trapped-ion laser cooling beyond weak Lamb-Dicke approximations.
why_it_matters: It gives a compact physical model for regimes relevant to faster ion control, where standard perturbative laser-cooling descriptions break down.
detailed_summary: The paper defines dark polarons as extended pseudospin-polarization states decoupled from a lambda laser configuration. In this representation, high-order Lamb-Dicke terms reduce to a single linear coupling that is independent of laser intensity. The theory is applied to explain cooling-rate limitations observed in high-intensity electromagnetically induced transparency cooling experiments.
main_result: The main result is a dark-polaron framework that captures high-intensity ion cooling and explains observed EIT cooling limits.
application_angle: Better modeling of strong laser cooling can improve trapped-ion reset, thermal management, and gate-cycle speed in quantum processors.

title: Low loss superconducting resonators enabled by aluminum microstructural engineering and dielectric trimming
abstract: Material losses in superconducting circuits fundamentally limit qubit coherence times and resonator quality factors. Most research efforts focus on mitigating losses at circuit interfaces, including metal--substrate, substrate--air, and metal--air interfaces. However, the correlation between TLS and non-TLS losses with the intrinsic properties of the superconducting metal and the dielectric edge smoothness is not well studied. In this work, we link the aluminum film grain size to non-TLS losses and the dielectric trimming profile and roughness to TLS loss; both loss mechanisms are subsequently mitigated. To reduce metal-related losses, we engineer the aluminum microstructure by heating during deposition, increasing grain size and reducing grain boundary density. Beyond mitigating metal losses, we introduce a two-step etching technique, Tropic etching, to suppress dielectric TLS loss by producing an ultra-smooth silicon surface with minimal defects and redeposition. These results lay out the fabrication pathway for aluminum resonators with lower loss, demonstrating two-orders-of-magnitude improvement in quality factor from $6\times10^{4}$ to $2.3\times10^{6}$. Since aluminum is the basis for most high-coherence Josephson junctions and dielectric edges are inherent to all common device geometries, the improvements in aluminum microstructure and edge profiling, presented here, can enhance the performance of superconducting quantum devices.
one_liner: Uses aluminum grain engineering and smoother dielectric trimming to raise superconducting resonator Q by about two orders of magnitude.
why_it_matters: It links specific fabrication knobs to TLS and non-TLS loss channels, giving a practical path to better superconducting quantum devices.
detailed_summary: The study connects aluminum grain size to non-TLS losses and dielectric edge profile or roughness to TLS loss in superconducting resonators. Heating during deposition increases aluminum grain size and reduces grain-boundary density, while a two-step Tropic etch creates smoother silicon edges with fewer defects. Together these process changes improve resonator quality factor from 6e4 to 2.3e6.
main_result: The demonstrated capability is a fabrication flow that boosts aluminum resonator quality factor by roughly two orders of magnitude.
application_angle: Because aluminum and dielectric edges are central to many superconducting qubit designs, the process can translate into longer coherence and lower-loss hardware.

title: The Threshold Theorem in Watts: Fault Tolerance as a Question About Objective Probability
abstract: In 2011 Hagar & Sergioli proposed a new interpretation of objective probability in deterministic physics. On it, the probability of a physical state supervenes on the resources, energy over time, required to realize it from a given state, relative to the resources available (arXiv:1101.3521). The motivation for that paper was an objective alternative to QBism, the view that sees quantum probabilities as subjective degrees of belief. Here I apply this interpretation to a more practical subject matter: fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). Under the resource-bounded measure Hagar & Sergioli proposed, the threshold theorem becomes a claim about classification: it asserts that error-corrected logical states belong to the class of relatively cheaply realizable states, whose probability remains near 1 as the machine grows. The theorem originally derived this claim from a resource inventory that was partial, and left out four resources consumed by error correction: calibration of a drifting device, decoding within the correction cycle, coherence as a finite time budget, and entropy flush through fresh ancillas. These entered the original derivation at zero price. Here I translate the feasibility of FTQC into a measurable quantity, watts per decade of suppressed logical error (a decade, in the engineer's usage, being one factor of ten in the error rate). I then show that the published record already contains its first data points for this translation, and I state the two measurements that would settle the question empirically. The three-decade debate on FTQC, conducted so far as an exchange about noise-model assumptions, turns out to be, under this interpretation, a quantitative dispute about a single object: the resource-bounded objective probability of the target logical states.
one_liner: Frames fault-tolerant quantum computing thresholds as a measurable resource cost: watts per decade of logical error suppression.
why_it_matters: It pushes FTQC feasibility debates toward empirical hardware metrics, though it is more conceptual and interpretive than a device result.
detailed_summary: The paper applies a resource-bounded interpretation of objective probability to fault-tolerant quantum computing. It argues that standard threshold-theorem reasoning leaves some physical resources effectively priced at zero, including calibration, decoding, finite coherence time, and entropy removal through ancillas. It proposes watts per decade of logical-error suppression as an experimentally measurable quantity for comparing FTQC feasibility.
main_result: The main result is a proposed resource metric that recasts FTQC feasibility as power cost per decade of logical-error reduction.
application_angle: The metric could help benchmark whether real quantum processors can scale error correction within practical power and cooling budgets.

title: Understanding interaction-driven transport in flux lattices with evolution-path symmetry
abstract: The destruction of Aharonov-Bohm (AB) caging by interaction and the emergence of interaction-induced chiral currents in flux lattices are two paradigmatic examples of interaction-driven quantum transport. While various mechanisms, such as bound-state formation and chiral spectral imbalance, have been proposed, a unifying physical picture remains elusive. Here, we employ the concept of \textit{evolution-path symmetry} (EPS) and its interaction-induced breaking as a framework to understand interaction-induced delocalization in flux lattices. EPS is defined as the invariance of a path's contribution under combined geometric and phase transformations. We demonstrate that in a $π$-flux rhombic lattice, interactions break the EPS present in the non-interacting limit by modifying the phase accumulation of many-body paths, thereby lifting the destructive interference responsible for AB caging. Furthermore, we apply this framework to explain interaction-induced chiral transport in flux ladders, where interactions break the phase relationship between symmetric paths, leading to a non-vanishing chiral current. Our work establishes EPS as a powerful tool for understanding transport phenomena beyond conventional eigenstate analysis.
one_liner: Evolution-path symmetry explains how interactions unlock delocalized and chiral transport in flux lattices.
why_it_matters: It gives photonic and synthetic-lattice experiments a clearer design rule for controlling interference-limited transport with interactions.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces evolution-path symmetry as a path-level interference principle for flux lattices. In a pi-flux rhombic lattice, interactions alter many-body phase accumulation and break the symmetry that enforces Aharonov-Bohm caging. The same framework explains interaction-induced chiral current in flux ladders through broken phase relations between symmetric paths.
main_result: The authors show that interaction-driven delocalization and chiral transport can be understood as interaction-induced breaking of evolution-path symmetry.
application_angle: The framework can guide engineered photonic or cold-atom lattices where transport is controlled by synthetic gauge fields and nonlinearities.

title: Substrate-metal interface engineering enhances TaN/Ta thin film superconducting resonator performance
abstract: Tantalum has been demonstrated as a promising material for superconducting qubits. However, comparatively little attention has been given to its nitrides. Tantalum nitride exhibits a range of stoichiometries, resulting in a variety of material properties, including both superconducting and non-superconducting phases. Owing to this versatility, tantalum nitrides can serve multiple purposes in superconducting qubits: as seed layers for alpha-Ta growth, as a superconducting base material and as a non-superconducting barrier in the Josephson junction. In this study, we explore the performance of superconducting TaN and Ta thin film combinations on silicon substrates in terms of internal quality factor Qi. We find that standalone TaN films exhibit Qi values of about 1.5x10^5 at 100mK in the single-photon regime. Surprisingly, a resonator made from Ta grown on a few-nanometers-thick TaN seed layer yields largely the same performance. However, adding an additional, few-nanometers-thick Ta buffer layer between the Si substrate and this TaN seed layer enhances Qi significantly up to 5.9x10^5. Supporting transmission electron microscopy measurements reveal nitrogen accumulation and structural disorder at the TaN-Si interface, while this interfacial modification is suppressed when the Ta buffer layer is introduced. The observed improvement in resonator performance is consistent with a reduction of interface-related two-level system losses and strongly supports the hypothesis that controlling the substrate-metal interface is pivotal for the performance of superconducting qubit circuitry.
one_liner: A thin Ta buffer layer at the Si interface boosts TaN/Ta superconducting resonator quality factors to 5.9e5.
why_it_matters: It identifies substrate-metal interface control as a practical lever for reducing TLS loss in tantalum-based superconducting qubit circuits.
detailed_summary: The study compares TaN and Ta/TaN thin-film superconducting resonators on silicon at 100 mK in the single-photon regime. Standalone TaN and Ta grown on a TaN seed layer reach about 1.5e5 internal quality factor, while inserting a few-nanometer Ta buffer below TaN raises Qi to 5.9e5. TEM links the improvement to suppressed nitrogen accumulation and structural disorder at the TaN-Si interface.
main_result: Adding a few-nanometer Ta buffer between Si and TaN significantly improves resonator Qi by mitigating interface-related loss.
application_angle: The result supports more robust materials stacks for superconducting qubits and microwave quantum circuits.

title: Metrology of quantum imaging schemes
abstract: We compare the performance of quantum imaging schemes based on spatially correlated photon pairs by formulating them as quantum multiparameter estimation problems, in which the object is characterized by transmission coefficients associated with different spatial modes. Our work focuses on standard quantum imaging techniques such as ghost imaging, two-photon imaging, and imaging with undetected photons. Specifically, we compute the quantum Fisher information matrices and show that they are saturated by Fisher information matrices corresponding to measurements in the object-mode basis, which generalize the common detection schemes employed in each imaging configuration. We find that ghost imaging and two-photon imaging generally provide higher precision for transmission estimation than imaging with undetected photons, but the latter is the only one that naturally does not couple transmission estimation across different spatial modes. These results identify which imaging protocols are best suited for specific tasks and provide practical guidelines for the design and optimization of quantum sensing technologies based on spatial correlations.
one_liner: Quantum Fisher analysis benchmarks ghost, two-photon, and undetected-photon imaging for transmission estimation.
why_it_matters: It turns quantum imaging protocol choice into a quantitative metrology tradeoff for spatially correlated photon-pair sensors.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates quantum imaging with spatially correlated photon pairs as a multiparameter estimation problem over object transmission coefficients. It computes quantum Fisher information matrices and shows object-mode-basis measurements saturate the corresponding bounds. Ghost and two-photon imaging generally offer higher transmission precision, while imaging with undetected photons uniquely avoids natural coupling between spatial-mode estimates.
main_result: The authors derive and compare precision limits for major quantum imaging schemes and identify measurements that attain them.
application_angle: The analysis gives practical guidance for selecting and optimizing quantum imaging protocols in sensing applications.

title: A route to damage tolerance exceeding $10\%$ in shuttling-equipped quantum processors
abstract: This is a short study of an approach offering high tolerance to damage (i.e. defects or 'drop outs') in solid state fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our method is primarily aimed at semiconductor electron spin-qubit systems, which have been shown to support fast and high-fidelity shuttling along pre-defined paths. We adapt the recent CAbLECAR method of Chadwick and Chong: stabilisers are performed by ancillas which each follow a bespoke pre-programmed path. We consider the simple surface code but we damage the physical lattice, and rely on route-solving software to find efficient pathways under constraints enforcing stabiliser commutation and hook error avoidance. Solutions are then converted to detector error models for Stim and logical error rates are obtained. We express our results by gauging the logical performance against that of a pristine lattice, using the notion of a reduced equivalent surface-code distance; for reasonable underlying error rates we find that $10\%$ damage leaves roughly half of the pristine equivalent distance ($d_\text{equiv}\approx0.48\,d_\text{pristine}$ in the large-array limit, rising to $\approx0.60$ for our smallest array). This suggests that one can tolerate substantial damage by building oversized arrays. We note that investigating damage tolerance of other qLDPC codes is a straightforward generalisation, and potentially one could adapt to damage emerging at runtime.
one_liner: Shuttling-based surface-code layouts can retain useful logical distance despite over 10% physical lattice damage.
why_it_matters: It suggests semiconductor spin-qubit processors can tolerate substantial device defects by routing ancilla shuttling paths around damage.
detailed_summary: The work adapts the CAbLECAR shuttling approach so stabilizer ancillas follow bespoke routes through damaged solid-state qubit arrays.
